CALL FOR LOWER INTEREST RATES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Inflation caused and aggravated by lack of production, along with higher interest rates and taxation like the excise tax on natural gas, means that farmers must pay more for heat, fertilizers, credit and machinery. Thus being unable to cope with these skyrocketing costs, they have no alternative but to cut production, which aggravates inflation bringing still higher interest rates, which again lowers production, all of which is already bankrupting our producers. Whereas the policies of the Liberal government are responsible for this vicious cycle, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper):
That this House demands that the Minister of Finance immediately lower interest rates for producers and eliminate the excise tax, which will start this country back toward economic sanity and stability, which will mean increased production, which will lower interest rates and inflation, which will again increase production, which will mean further increased production, which will lower interest rates and inflation, which will again increase production, and thus bring prosperity and happiness back to this depressed country.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT SOUGHT TO AID PART-TIME WORKERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Labour. In view of the fact that Canada's part-time workers, who are mostly women with family responsibilities, do not usually have access to fringe benefits or opportunities for promotion, can the minister say
what steps he is taking to ensure that those part-time workers who come under the Canada Labour Code can receive pro rated salaries and benefits, and that barriers to unionization are removed?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT SOUGHT TO AID PART-TIME WORKERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the question is a very pertinent one in today's society, and to a greater degree in view of the developments that appear will be occurring in the work force in the coming months and years. There are some companies which today hire, for certain classes of jobs, only part-time employees. Part of the reason for that may be the fact that they escape pension responsibilities. They are often able to hire those people at lower rates of wages, and there are other absences of benefits. As part of our review of the Canada Labour Code, my department is reviewing that situation and will be coming up with recommendations for legislation which might recognize in a more realistic manner what is happening in the work force today and what sort of protection might be provided for part-time workers, particularly female part-time workers who are a large part of that work force.

subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Postmaster General) moved
speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY
speechtext:
that Bill C-12, respecting bankruptcy and insolvency, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Madam Speaker, the bill on bankruptcy and insolvency whose second reading I have the honour to move today has indeed a long history behind it. It is the fifth such bill introduced before Parliament. Before explaining to the House

May 19, 1981
Bankruptcy
the philosophy and substance of the bill perhaps it might be useful to make a brief historic summary.
Back in February 1966, therefore over 14 years ago, the then justice minister who was responsible for the administration of the bankruptcy legislation ordered a full review of our statutes on bankruptcy. He requested a committee made up of public officials and experts to study the existing legislation and make recommendations about amendments which seemed advisable to them.
The current bankruptcy legislation dates back to 1949 and is in fact based on our 1919 legislation which in turn stemmed from the English statute of the last century. Of course the act of 1949 was amended to a certain extent in 1966. Those amendments were then made to fill an urgent and specific need, but an in-depth revamping of the bankruptcy legislation was postponed to a later date. That in-depth revamping is the object of this bill. Five years ago, in May 1975, when I was Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs I introduced the first version of this bill. Far was it from me to imagine that five years down the road I would again be called upon to introduce another version of the same bill.
It is obvious, and this has to be said, that protracted parliamentary procedures-the impossibility of a quick passage through the House of those bills deemed urgent but not necessarily priority items-did not help the implementation and adoption of this bill. Since the House of Commons had been unable to undertake consideration of the first bill in 1975, at my request the Senate banking, trade and commerce committee made an exhaustive study of the substance of the bill. After a number of study sessions during which many organizations made their views known, the Senate committee published in December 1975 a report recommending changes to many provisions of this bill. In light of that report, the first bill was substantially amended so as to include most of the amendments suggested by the Senate committee. Since then the bill has been reintroduced in the Senate, each time practically unchanged.
There was Bill S-ll in March 1978, Bill S-14 in February 1979, and Bill S-9 in November 1979, this time introduced by the minister of justice of the former government. The bill now before the House is identical to Bill S-9 of the last session that was brought in by the minister of justice in the Conservative government. It goes without saying that the act must meet the needs of the day, otherwise it is an inadequate tool that does not meet the objectives it was assigned or meets them inadequately. I need not insist on the fact that today's world of business and credit is not that of yesteryear and that, as a consequence, the Bankruptcy Act, as we now know it, was meant for days gone by, that it is not the instrument we need today to settle financial failures or regulate the rights and duties of the various parties involved. Let us remember merely
that the credit traditionally limited to the world of business and used by the ordinary citizen almost exclusively for the purchase of his home has now become commonplace for almost every citizen and to meet all sorts of needs, I would even say all sorts of whims on the part of the consumer. Consumer credit alone has shot up from $835 million in 1947 to almost $40 billion today.
It is no surprise then that in the face of that real credit explosion, the Bankruptcy Act should be resorted to increasingly and that it should become that much more imperative and necessary to bring it up to date. Any legislation on bankruptcy attempts to reconcile interests that are divergent by definition. It endeavours, on the one hand, to help the insolvent debtor or the overindebted find a way out of his financial difficulties. On the other hand, it seeks to protect, as it must, the interests of the creditors as equitably as possible, whose interests are contrary not only to those of the debtor but also to each other. Essentially, then, it is a special legislation with regard to normal legal relations between borrowers and lenders that provides for readjustments in legal relations between debtors and creditors. Those legal relations then are the ones this bill attempts to redefine more fairly and equitably in a context that is extremely different from the one in which the original act was passed many years ago.
I certainly cannot deny that this is a voluminous bill. It contains 420 clauses. In fact, it is a separate code which will contain, after future regulations are incorporated into it, all the provisions dealing with bankruptcy and insolvency. The first of the bill which I would like to underline is the distinction it makes between the way to deal with the ordinary consumer who is crippled with debts and the way to deal with business situations. Until now, there was no such distinction under the legislation except that a summary proceeding was allowed for small bankruptcies where the assets involved did not exceed $500. Under the proposed legislation, there would be two separate systems, depending on whether or not we were dealing with the insolvency of a consumer, which would allow us to deal adequately with two entirely different situations, the protection required in a commercial bankruptcy being different from what is required in a personal insolvency. I believe this is quite important because a very clear distinction will be made based on whether a consumer is involved or whether it is a company in financial straits.
Another aspect of the bill which I would like to draw to your attention is that it gives preference to arrangements over ordinary bankruptcies. Especially in the case of consumer bankruptcies, we prefer that an arrangement be made, whenever it is possible, rather than resorting to bankruptcy which, no matter what, is simply a confirmation of failure with all its implications. The proposed legislation contains twelve parts of different length, of course, but of equal importance. I would like briefly to deal with each one of these parts. Part I contains a great many definitions which serve to clearly establish the
May 19, 1981

scope of the legislation and to standardize some legal concepts. It establishes the prevailing importance of the act over any other act in cases of insolvency. Part II of the proposed legislation, which deals with the administration of the bill, establishes the administrative structure required for the implementation of such an act. The office of Superintendent of Bankruptcy, which has existed since 1932, will continue to do so, and will issue the licences to act as trustees to those persons who have the required qualifications. I would also like to mention that this Part contains provisions on conflicts of interest which constitute a code of ethics for trustees and inspectors.
Part III deals with arrangements for consumers. By definition, a consumer debtor is an individual who is insolvent, who may or may not be a businessman and whose debts, excluding a mortgage on his residence, do not exceed $20,000 or any other amount that may be prescribed in the future by regulation. This part establishes a simple and accessible system which would allow an individual who is burdened with debts to reach an arrangement with his creditors stating which portion of his debts he will repay. The next part deals with commercial arrangements. It consolidates the various procedures which are now found in many acts. The present bill is flexible in the sense that it allows a corporation which is in financial trouble but which is viable and worthy of being saved to file a proposed arrangement as circumstances allow.
The most remarkable change and undoubtedly the most interesting clause of the bill is the one which makes it possible for a debtor to file a notice of intention. Debtors more often than not do not think about submitting a proposal to their creditors when they are about to go bankrupt. We suggest that the debtor who is in trouble has neither the time nor the peace of mind needed to carefully work out a proposal likely to prove viable and acceptable to his creditors. That is why we have developed this concept of a notice of intention to file an arrangement. Under this clause, upon submission of a notice of intention to file an arrangement, there will be a 10-day stay of proceedings against the debtor, who will then have the respite he needs to draw up an arrangement at leisure. Another aspect of the commercial arrangements I should like to deal with is the new right which the courts enjoy to file a proposed arrangement where the debts of a corporation exceed one million dollars and where the proposed arrangement filed in respect of a debtor has not been accepted. As far as I know, the purpose of this clause is to do the utmost to save a corporation the folding of which could prove fatal to a community, a given area, a village or a town, if it is humanly possible to save it.
I admit that it is sometimes impossible and often economically undesirable to try to rehabilitate a corporation which is in trouble. Part V, I should say, deals with bankruptcy proper. I must say that we have seriously reconsidered the concept of bankruptcy, that we have maintained several elements which have proved useful in the past, but that we have brought about many changes. We are trying to set up a system which will be
Bankruptcy
consistent, self-contained and suited to the needs of today. All bankruptcy proceedings will begin with the filing of a petition either by the debtor himself if the bankruptcy is voluntary (which will replace the current voluntary assignment) or by one or more creditors if the bankruptcy is not voluntary (which will replace the current petition for receiving order). In the case of voluntary bankruptcy, the debtor's insolvency is the sole condition. Where it is not voluntary, the existence of admissible debts of at least $1,000 will have to be established.
When the petition is filed, all proceedings against the debtor by ordinary creditors are stayed and when the bankruptcy order has been made by the court, the exercise of the rights of secured creditors against the property of the debtor subject to the security interest is deferred for a period which may extend up to 40 days from the date of the bankruptcy order, depending on the date of the first meeting of creditors. However, the secured creditor can take the required remedies to protect his security. I have already noted that the bill aims at simplifying proceedings for the consumer. Part V of the bill includes section 163 that spells out special provisions for small consumer bankruptcies which exclude several proceedings required in a business context, but which are completely useless or at least unproductive in the case of a consumer, without, 1 repeat, depriving the creditors of their right to control the administration of the bankruptcy.
I would now like to say a few words about the effects of a bankruptcy on the directors and the officers of a corporation under this bill. The first effect is to declare the bankrupt unable to be a director or an officer of a corporation. The second is to make the directors and officers personally responsible for the debts of the corporation if its unsolvency was caused or aggravated by them or if they have mingled the property of the corporation with their own. The third effect is to make the directors jointly and severally responsible to employees of the corporation for unpaid wages at the time of the bankruptcy up to a maximum of $2,000 per employee, except if they establish their good faith. Finally, this part of the bill deals with the setting aside and review of certains transfers, whether they are entered into by persons who are or who are not at arm's length. In this area, the bill extends the application of the present legislation and promotes the fairest possible distribution of the debtor's property.
The next part, or Part VI of the bill, contains provisions applicable to arrangements and bankruptcy. The only provision in this part of the bill that I want to emphasize is the one which determines the order of priority held by each creditor in the distribution of the amounts produced when the bankrupt estates are realized. Except for funds collected on its behalf by a bankrupt, the Crown will become an ordinary creditor and will take its place among the other creditors and be paid at the same rate. This will increase the dividend of ordinary creditors, and we hope that it will prompt them to become more closely interested in the administration of bankruptcies.
I would like to revert to an aspect I mentioned briefly when I dealt with Part VI and which concerns the treatment given to unpaid workers. The first bill introduced in 1975 contained a

May 19, 1981
Bankruptcy
provision which granted absolute priority for unpaid wages on all the property of the bankrupt employer, including that subject to a security interest held by a secured creditor. This was an exceptional provision which went against the traditional rights of secured creditors, as of course several pointed out, and which, according to many, went too far and would not necessarily bring about the desired results. That is why it was suggested during the hearings of the Senate Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce that the creation of a special fund to compensate wage earners for wage losses caused by the bankruptcy of their employer would provide a more effective, a more practical and even a fairer solution.
The provision creating the foremost priority of the wage earner was then removed from the second version of the bill introduced in March of 1978. The ministers who presented each successive version of this bill have all stated their intention to have the issue of the timeliness and the desirable provisions of such a special compensation fund considered. Unfortunately, up to very recently this has never been undertaken. Accordingly, in order to be able to choose the best way of protecting the worker at the lowest possible cost without interfering with the financing structures of private business, I have decided to set up an inquiry committee to consider all the aspects of the issue and to report to me as soon as possible. This committee is currently considering the matter. It is chaired by the Dean of the Faculty of Law of the University of Ottawa and its other members are Mr. George Hitchmen, Vice-President of the Bank of Nova-Scotia, Mr. Ronald Lang, Director of Research for the Canadian Labour Congress and Mr. Raymond Dufour, a former high official of the Ministry of Industry and Commerce of the province of Quebec.
This committee of four which is made up of supporters of practically all viewpoints will have to proceed with great dispatch and report to me on what should be the best procedure possible. They will be given the chance of thoroughly studying the advantages and disadvantages of creating a special fund as the Senate committee seemed to advocate. They will naturally have to study the impact of such a fund on the already existing policies and legislation in those provinces which are concerned by this issue. I therefore expect to get that report this summer, by the end of June or early July. Then I will naturally be in a position to deal with the issue of the protection to be given to salaried workers in bankruptcy cases, an issue which I know is of some concern to members on both sides of the House and which, I hope, will find a solution before this bill gets through the third reading stage.
I think that this bill ought to be referred to the committee very shortly so that consideration of its 420 clauses may be undertaken and some progress accomplished so that we may benefit from the findings of this committee before proceeding with its final stage. At any rate, I think that the committee members who will study the bill in detail, clause by clause, will want to call Dean Landry before the committee in order to hear his opinion, his suggestions, when we come to the clauses
dealing specifically with wage earners who are not paid in the event of a bankruptcy.
I have just skimmed through the bill. In conclusion, I would like to say this: Parts VII and VIII of the bill specify the rules to be followed when securities firms or insurance companies go bankrupt. They were developed in close co-operation with experts in that field, and we have retained all the suggestions, all the recommendations they made in order to improve the present bill. Part IX deals with receiverships. The bill does not intend to restrain unduly the exercise of the rights of a secured creditor or of a trustee, but in cases of insolvency, it aims at subjecting them to a minimum of requirements to ensure that the rights of subordinate creditors are protected.
The three last parts of the bill deal with offences, the courts and evidence, and the transitional period from one act to the other. Mr. Speaker, I have given a brief overview of a bill that I will admit is very technical, but also very important. It is an attempt to reconcile interests that are not only different but conflicting. It does so as fairly as possible in my view. It is the result of endless hours of consultations and discussions with people associated with bankruptcies. Although not perfect, I am convinced it is as perfect as can be in the circumstances.
I commend this bill to the co-operation and support of honourable members from both sides of the House, so it may pass second reading and be referred as soon as possible to a standing committee, where honourable members can examine every aspect of the legislation and make a more detailed study of its various provisions. It is my hope the opposition will resist the temptation to score political points with the bill. This is a legal matter and it should be treated as such. It is not an economic matter at all and should not be related to the current economic conditions, I am aware that it would be easy to try to link consideration of the Bankruptcy Act with today's economic problems, but I suggest to hon. members opposite that the Canadian economic situation will not be solved by the Bankruptcy Act or any amendments to it. What we have before us is not an economic matter but a legal matter and it is my hope that those who speak after me will keep this in mind, and will postpone their criticism of the government's economic performance until some other time.
I believe that bankruptcies are one of this century's evils that in some respects may result from inflation. This bill however will not solve the problems of inflation. Indeed, it has nothing to do with today's inflation. The updating of the Bankruptcy Act is desired, it is called for by all parties concerned with bankruptcy, the administration of bankruptcies and legal matters pertaining to bankruptcy because amendments have long been overdue. And Canadian Parliament finally has an opportunity to study the act in the House of Commons; it has been amply studied in the Senate, in the other place, but finally it is considered here in Parliament and it is my hope that the discussion will indeed deal with legal matters rather than endlessly delving upon economic considerations. We must act expeditiously to send the bill to the committee of the House, where it will be scrutinized clause by
May 19, 1981

clause so that finally we may have a modern Bankruptcy Act in Canada as early as next summer, the summer of 1981.

subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks, I cannot help but comment that the persistently impoverished economic performance of this government should compel us all to act promptly with respect to this prospective legislation, as a record number of Canadian businesses and individuals within the next few weeks or months will be seeking the relief contained in this bill.
The bill before us today is, in fact, a culmination of more than 15 years of hard work with respect to our insolvency laws. It is necessary that we modernize commercial practices in terms of bankruptcy legislation. We must balance the priority of creditors. It is important that we streamline the administration of insolvency and bankruptcy legislation. It is important, also, that we correct the defects that exist in the present legislation.
The bill before us today has many excellent features and they are welcomed. Unfortunately, there still exist important aspects of the legislation which are totally unsatisfactory, such as the priority given to wage earners in a bankrupt estate and which must be rectified. I will have further comments with respect to this later in my remarks.
Bankruptcy is but one aspect of business failure. In addition, many companies that cannot meet their liabilities as they come due are put into receivership by their creditors. Still other companies exist as living corpses, unable to survive and they have to close their doors. I believe that it is important to recognize that in a free market economy there will always be failure; the weak and the inefficient will be weeded out.
What is of concern to me and to other members on this side of the House are the unnecessary business failures caused by the inept and ruinous economic policies of this government which crush the spirit of small businessmen, farmers and others who have a sense of commercial enterprise. I am not talking about the failures caused by management shortcomings or by overexpansion of a business or by fraud within a company; I am talking about the failures caused by high interest rates. In terms of today's rates, we formerly thought of these as being extortionary or unconscionable. I am talking about the inability of this government to create an economic environment which is conducive to investment and to commercial risk.
On the one hand, we have a Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) who tells the people of Canada that high interest rates are necessary in order to dampen consumer spending, while on the other hand his government has been the most profligate of all, consistently running up deficits, the accumulation of which has been the major source of inflationary difficulties in this country.
I think the Minister of Finance should make it clear to the people of Canada, while he tells them to curtail their consumer
Bankruptcy
spending habits, that this government has borrowed money on their behalf. We now have a gross national debt of $122 billion, of which each taxpayer's share is $13,700. If countries were run like companies and if individuals managed their finances in this way, you could bet your bottom dollar that this government would have been petitioned into bankruptcy a long time ago.
In my view, one of the problems with the economy is that we have a Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and a Minister of Finance neither of whom have any expertise in, or concept of, what it means to take a commercial risk. Neither has a tittle of personal knowledge of what it means to borrow in order to create and build a company or to take a mortgage in order to purchase a home. They have not chosen to build a business or had to mortgage a home, so it is small wonder that they are impervious to the anxieties of those who are on the edge of business failure caused by high interest rates, or to the frustration and concern of the man and wife who have to walk away from their home because they cannot afford to pay the interest on their mortgage, which has soared from 9 per cent or 10 per cent to 18 per cent in recent months.
Consumer and commercial bankruptcies are on the rise and, as and when this incredibly high interest rate is further absorbed into the economy within the next few months, we will see a toll of failures and tragedies such as we have not witnessed since the days of the depression.
Attitudes toward bankruptcies have changed dramatically in the last two decades, as is demonstrated by the record rate of increase in bankruptcies between 1960 and 1980. They have increased by a whopping 758 per cent. I wish to say more about the actual number of personal and commercial bankruptcies in a few moments, Mr. Speaker.
The point I want to make now is that the economic and social stigma formerly attached to bankruptcy has all but vanished. Formerly the disgrace of bankruptcy, more than the legal sanctions, kept many people from declaring bankruptcy. It is not only individual or consumer attitudes which have changed with respect to matters of insolvency; the credit system in particular, the explosive use of consumer credit in the past 20 years, has made possible the immediate purchase of goods through the instalment payment plan. By contrast, in 1960 the average consumer debt of every, man, woman and child was $224; in 1980 it stands at $1,532 per capita. The relaxation by government of laws insisting on minimum amounts of down payment and restricting the period of time over which the debt could be financed have contributed to this phenomenon.
It is also important to have a proper appreciation of how commercial lending habits have changed significantly during the past 15 years. Formerly, when a businessman went to a bank for the purpose of starting a business, as security for the debt the bank would take an assignment of the accounts receivable and a pledge with respect to the inventory of the business pursuant to Section 88 of the Bank Act. It was only when default occurred on the loan that the bank was permitted by law to require further security. In many instances the

May 19, 1981
Bankruptcy
debtor would be unwilling to pledge, for example, his machinery or his land.
As a result of the amendments to the Bank Act in the mid-sixties, banks are now permitted to take as security floating charge debentures which effectively form a charge on all the assets of a person's business. The commercial institutions own the debtor lock, stock and barrel. The real change is that when the banks call a loan and realize upon their security, they send in a receiver pursuant to the provisions of the debenture. Although the banks still take Section 88 security, common practice is that they realize under the terms of the debenture. That is an important point.
This has two practical effects. First, under the Section 88 security, banks are compelled by law to pay the wages of those who earned the wages. Under the floating charge debenture, there is no such obligation. Though it is the normal practice of banks to pay wages as a matter of policy, there are in some circumstances mutterings by persons who hold second or third charges behind the banks that the banks are spending their money.
The second consequence of the banks or other lenders realizing upon their security is that there is virtually no control over the duties and rights of the receiver. In a bankruptcy, a secured creditor is virtually untouched with respect to his legal rights. Although there is presently in the existing legislation the power of a trustee to request a stay of proceedings and the right to inspect goods, practice has demonstrated that the legislation is woefully inadequate in protecting the rights of both unsecured creditors and the debtor himself.
One of the most important aspects, in my view, of the bill is the provision delaying the ability of the secured creditor from realizing upon his security for a period of from ten to 40 days, depending upon the circumstances, so as to give the trustee an opportunity to inspect the goods, ascertain their value and decide whether or not he wishes to redeem the debt. What this prevents is receivers selling the security for bargain basement prices without some type of accounting to the unsecured creditor. The new bill further provides for the trustee to make a summary application as to the fees and disbursements of the receiver. This gives the trustee some practical control over the exorbitant charges that can be and are made in some circumstances. These provisions are important and are welcomed.
On the other hand, the treatment of wage earners in circumstances of a bankruptcy remains, under this bill, virtually unchanged. The wage earner is still a preferred creditor and ranks behind secured creditors and the cost involved in paying a trustee to administer a bankrupt estate. I am aware that under the proposed legislation a wage earner is now eligible to collect, if he can, a maximum of $2,000 instead of $500, and I am also cognizant of his ability potentially to collect up to $500 in pension contributions. Furthermore, there exists the right to sue directors for back wages. However, in my view, his position is inadequately protected. The history of the Bankruptcy Act has always been weighted in favour of the secured creditor. I believe that a much higher priority must be given to the man or woman who has earned wages at the time that insolvency occurs.
The minister will argue that the right to sue a director for wages is an important new right, but I point out to the minister that similar and even more onerous provisions already exist both in the Canada Business Corporations Act and most provincial business corporations acts. The point is that they are very rarely used. When the doors of a business are shut as a result of either receivership or bankruptcy, an employee wants and needs his wages then. He does not want to engage in costly litigation over a protracted period of time and where the chance of success is problematical, to put it at its highest standard.
Another method which is presently being considered and which has been under active consideration is the notion of establishing a wage earners protection act whereby both the employer and employee might contribute to the bankruptcy fund held by the government. I must say that I reject this method on a number of grounds. First, I am frightened by the prospect of the cost and the administration which would be necessary to make such a scheme viable. Second, it is foreign to me to imagine an employee contributing from his weekly or bi-weekly pay cheque to insure himself against the potential bankruptcy of his employer. I do not want to see any further creation of another layer of bureaucracy to administer such an insurance scheme.
Finally, what we could do is to give a real priority to the wage earner over the rights of the secured creditor. I know it will be argued that by doing so the banks will increase the cost of borrowing to the small businessman, and there is a fear, in some circumstances, that banks may not ever advance the money at all. However, I remind members that in every province west of the Ontario border there exists today a super priority legislation to protect the wage earner over the secured creditor. I do not believe that the cost of loans has been significantly affected in the western provinces. I believe the appropriate method is to take the suggestion of the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants that such wages be paid out of current assets of an insolvent estate not out of the machinery or land. Banks and commercial lenders have had the law weighted in their favour too long. Now is the time, in my view, to provide increased fairness to the wage earner specifically, and to unsecured creditors generally.
I want to direct some remarks to the new area called consumer arrangement. The bill contains provisions for the establishment of a government administrator whereby an individual whose liabilities are not in excess of $20,000 can make a proposal to creditors. This is a method designed to permit a debtor to pay a portion of his liabilities without going bankrupt, at the same time ensuring that his creditors receive more than they would under a bankruptcy.
There are some attractive features to this concept. There is no need to hire a private trustee. There are streamlining provisions to do away with mandatory meetings with creditors and there are further provisions for bankruptcy in the event of a three-month default in the payment of moneys called for
May 19, 1981

under the arrangement. The intention is good because the cost of bankruptcy has long been a serious concern to all of us in the House.
However, I suspect that when these provisions become well known and are publicized there will be an enormous flood of applications seeking this type of relief. The question which 1 pose to the minister today is whether or not there have been effective consultations with the provinces to administer such a scheme. My information, certainly as it relates to my province, is that there has been no agreement between this government and the province. More importantly, if my suspicion is correct, what is the cost going to be to administer such a scheme?
All of us in the House hope that this bill will reduce the cost of legal fees and administration fees in commercial bankruptcies. As it exists, trustees will not move in areas which are legally unknown; they seek the opinion of a solicitor or the advice of a court. But this need for their own protection, for legal opinions or the views of the court eats into the moneys that might be available to the unsecured creditor. One of the problems of the present act under which we now operate is that it is silent in so many areas. This new bill, with all of its 424 clauses, at least simplifies and gives direction to both trustees and claimants alike.
I am pleased to see the streamlining of administration which again avoids costs. For example, the provision that a discharge is automatic after six months, save where a caveat might be filed by an administrator, is an excellent feature of this bill. The legal costs of making a formal application for discharge, which is almost automatically granted except in circumstances of fraud, are thereby avoided.
1 must say that since 1967 most of the major insolvencies are not by way of bankruptcy, they are by way of receivership. Therefore, I am glad to see that under the new bill some statistics will be kept with respect to the number of business failures. It is important to understand that in all cases the superintendent of bankruptcy does not have the power to compile statistics with respect to receiverships. In view of the fact that most major insolvencies, such as Atlantic Acceptance and the Come-by-Chance insolvency in Newfoundland, are by way of receivership, it is important that we know how many business failures exist. I welcome the feature that statistics in this regard will be kept by the minister's office.

subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bankruptcy bill before us, as the minister has outlined, has had a very long history in this House. His presentation today indicated that this legislation was largely a housekeeping measure of putting a bill in place which had been under consideration for some long period of time and that it is really an amalgamation of old legislation and hopefully new procedures. The minister was very careful in his admonition to the opposition not to make this bill political or relate politics to this legislation. However, I submit that the situation with bankruptcy is political. There are other ways to examine this bill and maybe the issue of politics or making a decision by a group of people in public is the proper way to examine it.
Bankruptcy
There are two sides to this bill. The first side is housekeeping. My colleague who preceded me did an excellent job of pointing out certain strengths and weaknesses in this technical piece of legislation. The second side is important because it concerns the victims of bankruptcy.
I listened to the minister answer a question in the House today concerning the long-term causes of bankruptcy. He said that food in Canada, although extremely expensive and people are having difficulty coping, is much cheaper than in other places in the world where such things as starvation and infant mortality reign free. But the question is, how do the policies which this government is putting forward impinge on this legislation? I suggest that in bringing this bill forward at this point in time the minister and the government have their priorities crossed. For a long time this House has been asking for something that will deal with the causes of bankruptcy. We should not be doing an autopsy after the fact. The hon. member who preceded me and the other opposition party have pointed that out already.
This bill should probably be withdrawn immediately and the government should be dealing with the causes of bankruptcy. What we have before us is a piece of legislation which will deal with a situation which is largely being created by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the government, as the hon. member who preceded me has already pointed out. The Minister of Finance put forward to us an economic scenario showing the number of people who are suffering as a result of the economic situation. I want to delve into this for just a moment. It is a Catch-22 situation. The minister said the government recognized that interest rates are causing hardship and great difficulty but that the long-term benefit of high interest rates would be to bring down prices. However, they certainly are not doing that. Prices in this country are not coming down. The cost of goods and credit is being driven up higher and higher. The Catch-22 which the Minister of Finance set up was essentially put up for the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) in this bill. The high interest rate policy and the economic policies of this government will not bring down prices; they will increase prices and will continue to increase bankruptcies. It is amazing what this kind of logic creates. You can go back to the Irish potato famine which was a product of this kind of logic. I suggest to the minister we are not playing politics in this situation; we are asking for some basic common sense.
The government perceives this bill as a priority. It is not a priority; it is the conditions which create bankruptcies which are a priority of this House and the Canadian people. I suggest it is the government that is creating the bankruptcies. They should be looking at an economic policy which will prevent them, rather than put this legislation before the House at this time in an attempt to deal with the victims of bankruptcy.
There is one other aspect. Before we begin to look at a piece of bankruptcy legislation and resolve the problems for those involved, this government should be developing an interest rate

May 19, 1981
Bankruptcy
policy more in keeping with the needs of the people of this country. If the minister had any sense of priority about what is important in our economy-and Lord knows who made the decision to throw him into the breach and spend time on this bill-he would be bringing forward the competition legislation which has been promised since time immemorial. When the first competition bill came out in 1971, there was a commitment that we would deal with it in the spring. Now we are waiting for the fall and we will wait on and on.
One of the key problems in bankruptcies is the amount of corporate concentration in Canada. How does a small businessman compete against corporate supply control, market control and various other controls? We know the names of the individuals involved.
The hon. member who preceded me spoke about the increasing number of bankruptcies. This is because we have lost the environment for small business, with individuals being able to function in a free economy. This government has created a situation where there is a lack of competition. More and more businesses are being forced into receivership and bankruptcy. They are closing their doors and saying they cannot compete against the Thomsons and Southams and the kinds of corporate control we have in this economy. If the minister had any real sense of priority, instead of the Bankruptcy Act we would be dealing with competition legislation today.
The Bankruptcy Act is an important piece of legislation. It cleans up a lot of problems and expedites bankruptcy procedure. I wonder whether we are trying to deal with a principle or a priority?
With regard to the question of rising interest rates, it was mentioned in the House today that last year 14,000 people gave up their homes. Will there be another 14,000 giving up their homes this year because they have run into great difficulty? The minister should be dealing with the exorbitant credit charges which are causing bankruptcies. People are literally shutting down because this economy has put them under.
It is strange that the minister would today ask us not to play politics with this legislation considering the delays and sheer incompetence of this government in dealing with the real problems facing Canadians today. Those are the problems we should be dealing with. I would like the minister to explain to us why we have this bankruptcy legislation before us today. In our opinion, this bill is not a priority. Great relief would be expressed if the minister would withdraw this bill and submit legislation or policies to deal effectively with the problems facing Canadians today.
I next want to deal with the prevention of bankruptcies. Nowhere in the bill is the question of prevention of bankruptcies dealt with. In 1960 there were 1,000 personal bankruptcies. In 1980 there were 21,025. That does not include all the people teetering on the edge, those people who will go down when the interest rate goes up on Thursday as a result of following the American plan.
The number of bankruptcies is increasing dramatically. In 1980, 6,600 Canadian businesses folded up because of bankruptcy. That figure does not include receiverships and all the
rest. They left behind debts totalling roughly $1.2 billion. Price Waterhouse estimated that the loss to Canadians last year was between $5 billion and $10 billion. Neither the policies developed by the Canadian government nor the provisions in this bill deal with the whole question of prevention. There is a serious lack of logic in that approach.
It may be worth while to move on to another question and deal with some of the main problems. One of our most serious concerns is the matter of workers' wages. Possibly this legislation was put before us to fill an embarrassing gap in time rather than deal with something more productive. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has left, the Minister of Finance has left, and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is left holding the bag, so he threw in this piece of bankruptcy legislation.
I wonder why the minister brought this bill forward before it was rounded out and developed. The committee studying workers' wages has not even prepared an interim report. It is an ongoing committee. How can the minister place this legislation before the House when it does not even address the wages, benefits and pensions of workers? How can he bring the bill forward for second reading without dealing with that question? The government assumes they will have an interim report by this summer. The summer is virtually upon us. I suspect we will be looking at a recommendation in the fall.
Why are we dealing with this bill before that important point has been resolved? With the nature of the economy and the continuing high number of bankruptcies, Canadian workers will be put in a tremendously difficult situation. Before bringing forward this bill, the minister should have had something to offer the people of Canada in the form of protection. The responsibility for the increase in bankruptcies will be laid directly at the doorstep of the government. Increased bankruptcies will come about as a direct result of the government's high interest rate policies and the fact that the government has failed to bring forward competition legislation. This country does not have an industrial strategy which emphasizes support for Canadians. Because of that, Canadian workers and businesses will end up holding the bag.
1 suggest to the minister that, rather than finish this exercise on Wednesday, he hold off to see what further developments there will be. Possibly the minister could bring forward meaningful suggestions to the House of Commons about how we could deal with the question of bankruptcy, or he could urge his cabinet colleagues to do that. He could await the report of the committee which is studying the whole question of the priority of workers' wages.
Last week in the House we had a substantial debate on economic affairs in which the policies of the government were soundly criticized. The Minister of Finance, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and all hon. members opposite support programs leading to bankruptcies and weaknesses in the Canadian economy, yet on Friday the Prime Minister of Canada said at his press conference that in reality he did not
May 19, 1981

think the high interest rate program is working. As a matter of fact, it appears that the government is not really committed to dealing with the problem of people going bankrupt or the problems of the workers affected. How did we get into this position in the first place? Is the Prime Minister putting us on again as he did in 1975 with respect to the AIB? For three years the country was in absolute chaos, and then the Prime Minister finally came forward and said, "Sorry, friends, it was a good try, but it is not really working," and everyone said, "We told you so."
The economic policies of the government today are creating a large number of bankruptcies. If this bill ever goes through, it will be relied on to a very large extent. Even the Prime Minister thinks his high interest rate policy is not working. When will we give up and change the situation? When we will begin to adopt proper priorities in this House? When will we look to the prevention of bankruptcy and the protection of people who suffer most from it? I refer to families and working people whose wages, pensions and benefits accumulated over time and from long service are lost. Those services to companies and also to this country are rewarded by this government's leaving those people out to dry.
Another thing about which people have written is the ease of bankruptcy. Let us consider the plight of small credit unions when several people in a small community go bankrupt. Let us use the example of the community of Alert Bay. The big banks left there in a hurry because they could see what was happening during the fishing season, largely because of bad government management. Fishing activity was down and people's incomes were down. When several people go bankrupt, the only ones willing to serve communities financially are small credit unions. When people go bankrupt and leave debts and when there is no hope of returning the money to the community, credit unions suffer tremendously. They are not in the position of many of the larger institutions. On one day a fishing boat can be taken for collateral, but because of the market, the fishing industry and the way the government handles matters, the value of that boat can drop to virtually nothing the next day. Small credit unions are very seriously concerned about the ease with which people can go bankrupt. They are concerned about the loss of the funds they lend in good faith.
There is one other matter which concerns me. I have asked the minister about what he is doing to control credit. When people go into the Sears store, they are not asked to pay cash; people are encouraged to use credit. Gas companies and retail stores encourage people to use credit rather than pay cash or restrain purchases. Tremendous pressure is placed on people. People are being overburdened with charge cards, yet interest rates are jacked up from 18 per cent to 21 per cent and then to 24 per cent. This encouragement to use credit still goes on. It almost becomes a way of life.
The minister is not interested in controlling credit and exorbitant gouging which persistently goes along with it, to the point where people go under. They go bankrupt. The minister and the government appear to want to control credit by means
Bankruptcy
of bankruptcy. If people can declare personal bankruptcy easily and speedily, that will affect the economy and will not restrain the desire for credit. I submit that that is probably the wrong way to proceed. What we should really be doing is finding means of prevention, getting our priorities straight and looking seriously at controlling the tremendous blossoming of credit. According to the figures used by my colleague previously, over the last decade and a half the amount of debt has grown from roughly $200 to $1,500 per family. The amount of debt carried is enormous, and as high interest rates continue and as more people renew mortgages at these high rates, this will put many people under.
I know speakers from the prairies will deal with the small business proposals, but we nevertheless must protect small businesses from bankruptcy. We must deal with prevention. Not too long ago a group of farmers in Saskatchewan purchased some equipment in good faith from a dealer. When the dealer went broke, it was discovered that the farmers did not make their payments to the appropriate party. The farmers either had to pay twice for their equipment, turn the equipment back or, in some cases, close their doors and quit farming. That was a very serious situation. Small businesses will have to be protected from a government which seems determined that the easiest way to control inflation is by placing an enormous burden on Canadians and Canadian businesses.
There are three main areas of concern with respect to this legislation. One is the protection of employees' wages. If the minister had waited for that provision, the anxiety of many of us with respect to this bill might have been eased. This bill might have had a chance of going to the committee fairly soon. If the minister had dealt with the question of the ease of bankruptcy and its effect on small communities and if he had dealt with other subsidiary problems communities have, then perhaps the bill could have gone to the committee sooner. If some attention had been given to the question of protecting small businesses from government policies, perhaps the bill could have gone to the committee much more rapidly.
I suggest, in summary, that putting this bill before us today was a political decision of the government. It was a callous, calculated decision of the government. Hon. members opposite did not want to talk about the matters which were raised last week in this House. Those matters are of serious concern to Canadians who live out there in the real world. This government has talked about the Constitution and anything but the real, gut issues affecting the people. The government has avoided dealing with the prospect that more bankruptcies will occur this year. I suggest that the bringing forward of this bill was a calculated, political manoeuvre in order to avoid dealing with the issues that are important to us. This bill is premature and ill-conceived.
The second priority should be the prevention of bankruptcies. An enormous number of people will have to renew their mortgages this year. Instead of renewing at 10Vt per cent, they will be renewing at 18 per cent, or perhaps 19 per cent or 20 per cent, who knows? Certainly the government does not know.

May 19, 1981
Bankruptcy
What will that do with respect to personal bankruptcy? Small businessmen are now trying to operate at interest rates of 19 per cent and 20 per cent on their revolving credit. What will that do with respect to summer employment? We have a very serious problem. The priority should be prevention of bankruptcies, and we should be dealing with the key problems.
Other people will be speaking about this in the Elouse today, tomorrow and the following days while this bill is before us for discussion and about other bills we may be considering while the government fills the gap before talking about the real issues.
1 see that my time has almost expired, Mr. Speaker, so 1 will allow someone else to speak at this point.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thought the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Evans) was going to give us his words of wisdom at this point.

speechtext: You could certainly use them.

subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY
speechtext:
I share the feelings of the hon. member of the New Democratic Party who expressed surprise and anger at the bringing forward of Bill C-12 at this particular time, given the state of the economy in Canada. I differ with the hon. member, however, when he suggests that the government should withdraw it. Goodness knows, if they are not going to do anything about the deplorable economic situation these incredible interest rates are going to cause, then perhaps doing something to cushion the fall for those victims of the system is marginally better than doing nothing. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the timing of this particular bill is almost a cruel joke.
Last Thursday many of us here were visited by about 125 businessmen from the energy service industries of Alberta and Saskatchewan who came to Ottawa to try and explain to the government and members of Parliament the difficulties they were having maintaining and sustaining their companies in view of the impact of the National Energy Program. The feeling among the 125 different companies represented in this delegation was that if this program is not amended drastically within six months, 50 per cent of them would be out of business. Within a year, 75 per cent would be out of business and perhaps bankrupt as a result of this government's energy policy.
So what we have, Mr. Speaker, is some very concerned Canadian businessmen, in most cases proprietors of their own firms, small and medium-size firms in the energy service industry, coming to Ottawa and saying: "Look, stop what you are doing, you are driving me into bankruptcy; I have to lay off employees now". On average, those firms had already laid off 25 per cent of their employees. They said: "Unless you do something, unless you straighten out your act in regard to energy policy, we will be out of business and bankrupt in six months". The response of the government is to bring in amendments to the Bankruptcy Act to make it easier for them
to go bankrupt, rather than looking at the root of the problem. Indeed, in today's question period the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. MacLaren) still denied the problem exists, which is the most insane form of myopia that we have seen from this government for some time.
According to a document issued by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the background paper on the bankruptcy and insolvency bill, during the 1970s the number of bankruptcies in Canada, essentially static, commercial bankruptcies, was around 5,000 a year. This represented the number of companies which, perhaps for reasons of poor management or too fast growth, or perhaps due to circumstances beyond their control, went out of business.
In the last three years that situation has changed dramatically. In 1980, for example, there were 6,595 commercial bankruptcies, up 17 per cent over the 5,600 in 1979. In the first quarter of 1981 bankruptcies are up 20 per cent over the comparable period in 1980. This is tremendous growth. Indeed, the only thing growing in the economy today seems to be the jobs of accountants and lawyers specializing in bankruptcies; they experienced a 17 per cent growth last year and 20 per cent so far this year, and we have seen nothing yet compared to what is coming unless something dramatic is done, and done very soon, about interest rates.
Clearly the number of commercial bankruptcies this year will be well in excess of 8,000, more likely 10,000, and yet as the spokesman for the New Democratic Party pointed out the reaction of the government is to say to the people, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said the other day: "But you are way better off; you are 50 per cent better off than you were ten years ago." Now, 1 am sure that is a lot of comfort to the 8,000 or 10,000 businesses that will be going bankrupt this year, not to mention the employees who will lose their jobs as a result and the creditors who will not receive the money owed them. In fact, the only ones who will be cheering are lawyers and accountants specializing in bankruptcy.
As an aside, Mr. Speaker, I would like to see some political scientist do an estimate of the impact of our activities in this House, because I figured out that I spend about 50 per cent of my time here making work for lawyers and accountants. I sure wish we could change that a little bit and perhaps spend some part of our time creating opportunities for Canadians, making life better for them rather than making work for lawyers and accountants.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the human costs of bankruptcy are incalculable. As my colleague the hon. member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer) pointed out, there is no question there has been attitudinal changes occurring in our society over the last few years whereby the stigma attached to bankruptcy perhaps is not what it used to be. We no longer have debtors prisons. Nonetheless, the stigma is still there and it affects those who should least be affected.
May 19, 1981

Granted, because of changes in our society there are people who in the normal course of conducting their personal affairs are not perhaps as prudent as we might like, or as may have been the case in days gone by; but the thought of going bankrupt is not greatly feared, and many people do indeed declare bankruptcy on a personal basis without losing a great deal of sleep over it and seem to start up again. However, to the prudent and responsible kind of person we would probably describe as the backbone of our country, bankruptcy represents a horrendous personal defeat. In many cases it represents loss of self-confidence and self-esteem, the costs of which are incalculable. It leads to family break up, in some cases to suicide and to all kinds of tragic human loss. As a nation we certainly cannot afford the loss of jobs and potential growth that will result from these commercial bankruptcies.
In addition, in the first quarter of this year there have been 75 farm bankruptcies. The cost of that to the country is inestimable. It is certainly tragic to have a government come forward and say: "Well, what we really have to do, people, is take a look at this Bankruptcy Act; we have to streamline it after 15 years. Do not worry, the question of the economy, of interest rates and business activity is not something we should discuss right now; we can do it another time." Well, we wonder when that other time will be, Mr. Speaker. We wonder when we will get some action out of the government with regard to the economy, and we wonder when the question of the causes of bankruptcy will be addressed in the way it should be.
I should emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that when I talk about bankruptcies I mean formal bankruptcies, not the insolvency that comes as a result of receivership which ends up leaving a financial corpse at the end. As the hon. member for Cambridge pointed out, the vast majority of business insolvencies is through receiverships, not bankruptcies, as a result primarily of the banks and other financial institutions imposing receiverships upon commercial enterprises through floating charge debentures which are now a standard part of the banking business. I will have a little more to say about that later, but in looking back I think the Parliament of Canada made a tragic mistake in its amendment of the Bank Act which allowed the banks to employ floating charge debentures as a method of financing business enterprises. The abuse in that area has been tremendous. While there are some steps in the proposed legislation to prevent perhaps some of the abuses which have occurred, I do not think they go far enough. In any case, we will want to examine that matter very closely at committee stage.
I read with interest the background paper on the bankruptcy and insolvency bill prepared by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. I noticed that the process started in 1966 with an internal study committee which perhaps put forward most of the proposals which are now incorporated in this bill, although they have been augmented and amended as a result of various studies of its earlier manifestations as Senate bills.
Bankruptcy
The study committee made one recommendation which was not accepted by the government, that is, the recommendation that the private sector trustees be replaced with public sector ones. 1 find myself in a bit of a quandary, not being a great fan or believer in the efficiency or effectiveness of government as opposed to that of the private sector in conducting business. I am concerned about the use of private sector trustees because there is very little incentive for efficient, effective and speedy performance by public trustees, whether in bankruptcy or in receivership. Private sector trustees are in the business of providing a service. They get paid when they provide the service. In most commercial cases the trustee is, in fact, a corporation which employs professionals such as lawyers and accountants for whom a per diem or a fee of anywhere from $75 to $200 an hour is necessary.

speechtext: To make it last.

subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY
speechtext:
Consequently, when they are assigned as trustees of an enterprise or an estate with significant resources, there is all the incentive in the world to make it last, as my colleague points out. There is an incentive to keep it going and to justify the $200 per hour fee for lawyers and accountants; it is a very lucrative business. I do not see any incentive in the proposed legislation for the trustees to do anything else but to sit there and collect fees. Ultimately the estate or enterprise is bled dry and runs out of resources, in which case there is no longer anyone to pay the fees and it is wound up very quickly. It is regrettable that we do not have firm data on this, but from the talk one hears from people on the street and those visiting constituency offices who have been victims of such situations, one gets the impression that many trusteeship situations are wound up precisely at the time the last dollar has gone.
In many situations, a speedy and efficient transaction of business at the initial stages of the insolvency could have resulted in there being left a viable entity, albeit diminished, to carry on business. It almost never happens, once a trustee becomes involved, that after a few weeks or months there is an ending of the trusteeship or receivership in a manner which leaves in place a viable, ongoing enterprise.
In the case of formal bankruptcy trusteeships, there is the provision of the supervisor of bankruptcy of the bankruptcy branch of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Also there is a licensing provision in regard to trustees. Presumably the supervisor can weed out incompetent trustees or keep an eye on their behaviour. At least he could listen to complaints and perhaps do something about them. As I pointed out, from the things I hear on the street it does not happen very often.
In the case of a receivership where a bank moves in by virtue of its floating charge debentures to seize the operations of a commercial enterprise, the incentive to ensure there is not a nickel left is overwhelming. The only recourse of the estate or a debtor for inefficient, ineffective or for that matter illegal or immoral behaviour, is through the civil courts by launching an action. Therefore, once a receiver gets his hands on an

May 19, 1981
Bankruptcy
estate on behalf of a bank, it is in the interests of the bank and the receiver to ensure that nothing is left in order to provide the resources for launching a civil suit against the bank or the receiver by the proprietors, directors, owners or whoever had an interest in the estate.
I am not suggesting that this is the way it always happens or that every bank or receiver has that motive in mind, but I am suggesting that this is the incentive which is provided in the current situation. 1 think it is bad law to have a situation which provides such an incentive. Instead, we should be looking at law which provides an incentive for a receiver or trustee to be as efficient and effective as possible, to recover for the creditor the moneys owed as quickly and painlessly as possible, and to leave in place as much of the assets as possible for other creditors or perhaps to maintain an ongoing entity.
It is unfortunate that we do not have hard evidence in this regard, but I can relate at least one anecdote of a fellow who came into my constituency office to complain. The man was in the seismic business. He had a very substantial seismic operation, including offshore seismic equipment and a ship. He employed 30 or 40 people. He owed the bank a certain amount of money, as does anyone who is in business or in current operation. The bank had the loan secured under a floating charge debenture. In this case, again as a result of government policy changes, he had some contracts cancelled very quickly which left him in a liquidity crunch. The assets of his company exceeded his liabilities by a substantial amount, but the assets were tied up in a ship and in high-priced seismic equipment. He told me the banks demanded payment on a Friday. Obviously, on a Friday afternoon he could not raise any funds and later that afternoon he was in receivership. Within the month his equipment had been sold at fire sale prices. The bank recovered the funds owed to it and he was out of business. He saw his life's work and several million dollars blown out from beneath him. The purchaser of the equipment and the boat did very well, but that was of small comfort to my constituent.
I do not know whether this story typifies what happens to others, but according to the Canadian Federation of Independent Business this kind of situation happens more often than they would like to see. Apparently the federation's membership has experienced similar circumstances to the ones outlined by my constituent. I understand the federation is conducting a study of bankruptcies, and perhaps representatives of that organization will be appearing before the committee to offer their advice.
In any case, this legislation is welcome. As a result of it data will be collected on the different kinds of insolvencies so that we will know what costs are involved. We need to examine ways in which we can provide an incentive to trustees or receivers to act with some dispatch. Public declarations of the fees collected and declarations of the transactions involved in terms of the disposal of assets are two incentives which come to mind. Perhaps more cases should be allowed to go to
arbitration. As matters stand now, the receiver really becomes God when he walks into a commercial establishment. Perhaps there should be a check on the receiver's behaviour by the creditors, the proprietors or the management with the possibility of some sort of arbitration to resolve matters, rather than the trustee or receiver having the last word at every stage. I do not know the answers, Mr. Speaker, but I do think there is a problem here which should be addressed. Complaints have been too widespread to dismiss them as lacking any substance.
I commend the proposed legislation in regard to its emphasis on the ability of a debtor to make arrangements, whether it is a consumer debtor or a commercial debtor. Without having any hard facts before me, it strikes me that the Americans, through their chapter 11, as they call it-which is basically a reorganization similar to the arrangement proposed in this legislation-seem to avoid major commercial bankruptcies in a way that heretofore we have not done. It seems to me that if the banks and financial intermediaries would agree to arrangements, as opposed to receivership, we would see fewer devastating ends to commercial enterprises, something which is becoming all too common.
We have been treated to several news programs on television of late showing that banks send trucks on to farms early in the morning to haul off the livestock to slaughtering plants. They have sold breeding stock for bacon at prices from ten to 50 times lower than its real value. Hopefully this kind of behaviour, which is permitted under the current legislation, will be curtailed through the use of the measure before us. The arrangements under the legislation before us will ensure that the banks get their money back, but it will also ensure that the debtor is not punished unduly.
The provisions in the proposed legislation vis-a-vis wages of employees is welcomed, although, as my hon. friend pointed out, we might well wish to strengthen this provision in committee. We believe that people who have earned salaries should not be placed in secondary positions to banks and financial institutions or, for that matter, other creditors.
In conclusion, I must say again that I am constantly amazed by the crust, if you will, of this government in choosing to bring in an amendment to the Bankruptcy Act, at a time when we have record high interest rates which are almost unfathomable in terms of size, at a time when businessmen are wondering how in blazes they will be able to pay the interest on their debts at 20 to 24 per cent-these MacEachen rates are astronomical-at a time when bankruptcies in the first quarter of this year have increased 20 per cent over last year, when farming bankruptcies have increased by 73 per cent in the first quarter of this year as compared to the same period last year, at a time when Canadians fear for their economic future.
I must admit that the gall of this government is something to behold. There seems to be no limit to its arrogance or its crust. The feeling seems to be that it is the natural governing party, that it knows what is best and that the rest of us should keep our peace. We are being told that we are better off than we were ten years ago and that farmers are doing better now
May 19, 1981

than they were before. According to the Prime Minister, everything is hunky-dory and the government will set its own priorities. Never mind that you cannot afford to renew the mortgage on your house, never mind that the bank has just seized your farm, never mind that the company you work for may go bankrupt; never mind all these things, we are just to follow the government's agenda because it knows best. 1 do not think it does.
As long as the government House leader sets the agenda in this House we have no choice but to debate what he puts before us, and we will continue to debate the government's priorities. We hope that this legislation will not be unduly held up. It is an improvement to the existing legislation, and it can be further improved. The government can be sure that it will receive co-operation from this party in order to make it a better measure for all Canadians.
