The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Ouellet that Bill C-12, respecting bankruptcy and insolvency, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
Bankruptcy

subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are finally getting a new bill respecting bankruptcy. I know that this has been a subject of discussion for several years. I have been sitting in this House for 25 years and I remember that the representatives of the provinces have been negotiating with the federal government in order to come to some arrangements such as those provided in this bill.
At one time bankruptcy did have a very serious stigma; but events have taken place over the past 60 years which have changed the public's conception of bankruptcy. Prior to and during the 1920s the man who went bankrupt was a total failure. It was a disgrace. In fact, I can recall that at that time a farmer could not be made bankrupt. This provision that a farmer could fall under the Bankruptcy Act only came about in 1949. During the 1930s we saw introduced the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act which had great application during the 1940s and 1950s. As a young lawyer, I inherited a whole portfolio of files dealing with foreclosure. That is where 1 cut my teeth, on foreclosure practice, when I was dealing with old FCAA files.
There was a great deal of tragedy involved in many of those files. I recall what was told to me by my then senior partner who had a great deal of experience and was a very kindly man, and some judges and trustees who had dealt with farmers and, as well, not only small businessmen but business as a whole during the 1930s. They said bankruptcy was the best thing that these people could go through because it took a mountain off their shoulders, one which they would never have been able to shed, and gave them an opportunity for a new start. So far as farmers were concerned, many a time was an arbitrator, usually a judge, named to supervise adjustments of debts, whereby land debts, overdue grocery accounts, twine accounts, oil accounts and what have you were all written down. It was a proposal much as we see in section 3, the consumers' section of this present bill. Many a farmer had an insurmountable load taken off his shoulders. Prior to the arrangement, the wall he faced had seemed sky-high, but now he could begin to see over it. With changing economic conditions, these people were able to continue and get out from under, but something had had to be done. I think, to that extent, the old FCA Act was a good piece of legislation, certainly so far as farmers in western Canada were concerned. That is where my experience came from, even though 1 came on the scene late. It was the only answer.
How about businesses in the 1930s? I know that in the province of Alberta some of our leading corporations went through the wringer of bankruptcy in 1933, 1934 and 1935. They got rid of their debts caused, in many instances, because they had done work but had not been paid. There were many construction firms which had done the work but they could not get paid. Why could the owners of the buildings not get paid? Because they could not rent them. There was no revenue coming in. The whole economy as we knew it had almost come

May 19, 1981
Bankruptcy
to a grinding stop and something had to be done. It is no pleasure for bank managers to contemplate ledgers where notes are piling up interest which will not be collected. There is no way a wholesaler can continue giving credit to a merchant who can sell but cannot get paid; and it goes on, all the way down the line. So I think the 1930s taught a lot of people about bankruptcy and compilation of debts and arrangements.
We are talking about consumers in section 3, those whose debts outside of a family residence mortgage do not exceed $20,000. Many of those people cannot be put through a bankruptcy proceeding. They do not have the money or the assets to pay trustees or lawyers. However, do not think for one moment that this is a new-found gem or that the people in consumer and corporate affairs have come up with a brilliant idea within the last while. A section of this kind was in place and operating in the province of Alberta in the early fifties.
I forget the precise name of the legislation, but strangely enough a good friend of mine is a director of that section of the attorney general's department which administers this legislation. He was then also in that position. He had a great deal of experience. In my early years in Ottawa, I do not know how many times he came down to discuss with the federal authorities the incorporation into federal legislation of some of the principles and regulations of the legislation with regard to consumers. Thank goodness it has come!
We will see, when we are in committee and able to discuss the precise regulations, just how it is proposed that we deal with what I consider to be a vast horde of people. Incidentally,
1 think their numbers would increase if they knew they could go to experienced counselling officers under a debtors' assistance board so that their affairs could be examined, they could be advised, and they could be kept to arrangements made with their creditors. In the main, creditors are honourable people who have not necessarily lent any money but who may have advanced credit for the sale of goods and services. They are unpaid vendors. True enough, there may be some finance companies, banks or other retail credit organizations that have assisted in furnishing credit.
Today we have massive international credit cards which become almost a temptation for people to go out and spend. We are in an economy that depends upon buying and selling for the production of goods and services so that salaries may be paid and people may then purchase other goods and services. This is part of the economy. If you have ever heard a big truck come to a grinding halt or slow down as the result of shifting into a much lower gear, that would be nothing compared to the noise of the North American and western European economy if credit cards and credit buying were eliminated. When looking at the money supply today, one should not only look at the cash that is in circulation, at demand deposits and at cash on hand in the banks, but also at the total amount of goods bought and outstanding credit purchases.
If hon. members have money in a bank account, it matters little whether that money is there as a result of deposit or
whether they borrowed money and put it in the account. Master Charge, American Express, Visa and the credit cards of the major oil companies and department stores are all the same; one card is as good as $300 in the pocket at any time.

subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY
speechtext: Never!

subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY
speechtext:
The cards can buy goods at quickly as cash can. As a matter of fact, it is easier to buy with a credit card than with a personal cheque. They should be part of the money supply. When we look for reasons for inflation, the total amount of the wherewithal on which our economic machine turns should be considered. Credit cards are a relatively latter day phenomenon. People are indebted to the credit card companies as a result. This is not the fault of these companies nor of the banks which issue the credit cards, however; the purchase is made by the individual. John Citizen has to accept the blame for a lot of his own problems with overextended credit.
There are all sorts of reasons why consumers overextend their credit. They may have made a mistake; perhaps the payments were too high; perhaps there were two breadwinners in the family and for one reason or another one lost a job or had to resign. In any event, the income is not sufficient to meet the monthly payments. Then there are those who want to live higher than their income would permit. That is also a mistake in judgment. They are the people who play around with credit accounts, paying two months out of three, or three months out of four, and never asking the same creditor to absorb two delays in a row. You cannot call that kiting; they are playing a game of roulette with their creditors. That is all right if they do not become involved in more debt, but that type of individual can rarely resist the temptation to get into debt. They buy today in anticipation of paying with tomorrow's inflated dollars.
It is a very simple psychosis that a man who buys merchandise on credit today that is too expensive for him anticipates having it paid for in two years when he expects to be earning 25 per cent or 30 per cent more than he is earning today. He does not content himself with buying on credit, however; next year he goes on a holiday. That is the type of individual who ends up as a consumer debtor under this particular legislation. I am not going to cry crocodile tears for that individual.
Having said that, we must ask how we can deal with the situation. We cannot ignore those individuals because there are tens of thousands of them in the country. Their situation is almost like that of a doctor who would say that he is going to neglect all cases of measles or the common cold. It cannot be done. Instead, he must try to eliminate measles and the common cold. In this particular case, the solution is not up to John Citizen who owes $20,000. Actually, I do not think that is enough and I hope there is provision for increasing that amount by way of regulation, because with inflation as it is at present, $20,000 will be out of date by the time this legislation is passed. Let us be satisfied that we can convince this individual that he should go to see the equivalent of a debtor's assistance board run by the federal government, not the prov-
May 19, 1981

ince. I see that there is provision for this in the act. The thrust seems to be that this board will be under provincial administration. That is the way it should be. It should be done with as little formality as possible.
My colleague the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) spoke about trustees and receivers. We know about those. 1 am reminded of when 1 was a young lawyer. Someone presented me with an old British cartoon showing two lawyers on the chancery side of an estate. Both of them were talking over a particular estate saying that it would be a pity if any of the beneficiaries got anything. Outside of perhaps priority creditors, such as the Government of Canada with its claim for unremitted income tax, unremitted unemployment insurance and unremitted Canada Pension Plan deductions, we have seen commercial and industrial bankruptcies where the creditors have received very little. But if you looked at the trustee's fee and the fees for solicitors who were acting on behalf of the trustee, you would see that was where the money was wrung out. But those men are entitled to do the work and to get paid for it.
I do not share all of the views put forward by my colleague from Calgary, because it seems to me we have been able to protect some very complicated bankruptcies. As a lawyer I used to do a certain amount of that work on behalf of creditors. If there were a sensible judge who knew something about a business, one who could be reached in a minimum of time who could give decisions and understand proposals, perhaps a proposal for the bankrupt concerned to continue operations but with supervision, this might be beneficial. I think that should be the case in many so-called bankruptcies today.
I see there is provision in the act for commercial arrangements and the possibility of a trustee being appointed by the court to work along with management on behalf of management's interest and on behalf of the creditors. After all, a going business is the only one that has a chance of making any money and of keeping people employed. On the other hand, a padlock on the door means the end of the road to a great many people. I think far too many padlocks get used. Perhaps there should be an opportunity for continued operation of businesses. They do it in the United States. If my memory serves me correctly, under what they call Section 11 multimillion-dollar concerns are able to make proposals, along with trustees appointed by a court, for operations to continue. There have been many cases where, in the end, creditors come to some sensible arrangement. Perhaps they are prepared to accept 75 cents, 80 cents or even 50 cents on the dollar knowing that is as good as they will ever get from their previous commitments. If a company gets rid of a heavy debt load it may yet be in a business whereby new owners with new ideas and more capital would be interested in taking over. There are many possibilities.
If anyone wants to take a good look at this act, it represents over an inch of paper in thickness. This act is complicated. What is more, the back sections, which include the schedules
Bankruptcy
and the annexes, create some of the difficulties and confusion because they amend other legislation. We see that the Bank Act is going to be amended. I do not think it affects Section 88 but it may affect the banks' secured position. I am not aware that there is a great deal of change in the priorities of creditors except perhaps in so far as employees having claims for unpaid wages are concerned. They do not rank ahead of secured creditors. Their ranking is among preferred creditors, but behind Crown Canada.
In situations where there were unremitted income tax deductions, the Crown has said that money was held in trust by you, the firm, on behalf of the Crown with respect to tax owed by Mr. X or Miss Y. The same may be said about unemployment insurance, Canada Pension Plan contributions and federal sales tax. These are all preferred claims ahead of unsecured creditors.
Now comes the question of wages not paid to employees. There is mention of a sum of $2,000 with a further sum of $500 in certain circumstances. If my memory serves me correctly, in priority $2,000 was the maximum in wages an employee could claim for something like four to six weeks, I forget which. That provision was in the 1949 act and wages were much less then than they are now. Wages were not defined in a maximum amount. I would think it would be advantageous if in the committee hearings we changed this provision from $2,000 to a weekly salary. Within three or four years, $2,000 may be totally inadequate. It would be better to say simply that an unpaid employee shall be entitled to four or six weeks' full salary, whatever the decision is, after the appropriate deductions have been made from that salary for unemployment insurance and so on. Incidentally, they would have to recover enough money to pay income tax, CPP and other statutory deductions from those salaries so that the employee can get full credit.
There is another area in which there has been a lot of criticism of trustees and receivers, as though they work behind curtains, away from the creditors and debtors and as though there was something mysterious about their operation. I am not satisfied with the way trustees were named previously. There always seemed to be an element of political patronage which I did not like. Over the years, it was often easy for a Liberal to come here and be named a trustee in bankruptcy but very difficult for anyone else. I suggest that lends some credence to the suggestion that the trustees and lawyers would divide the estate and the creditors and owners would get what little was left over, if anything.
I would prefer that every bankruptcy be supervised by a properly educated judge, someone who knows something about business, to whom the trustees would have to report fully. In some jurisdictions, through an arrangement with the provinces we could have a bankruptcy court or division, if the volume merited. At least there would be supervision. Anything that is supervised and out in the open has much less chance of being unfair.

May 19, 1981
Bankruptcy
One example is the construction business. If an apartment building goes blouey part way up and no more money is available, the mortgagee may refuse to extend further credit. All too often the major creditor is in a position to arrange new financing for the continuation of the project, having squeezed out the others. There is a sale by the trustee to a nominee of the major creditor or to an affiliated company. The small creditors get squeezed out. This may mean an awful lot to them. All too often it is the mid-range creditor, those involved to the tune to $50,000, $75,000 or $100,000, who take the brunt of these failures. These people must be protected as well.
I admit there is no way that everyone can come out of a bankruptcy with no loss. If the employees have been careful and have insisted upon being paid up to date, they will be covered by the statutory protection. A secured creditor will undoubtedly be protected, unless there is some great misfortune. However, that secured creditor should not be able to sell the property at a distressed price; it should be at a reasonable market price so there is some residue. What I am saying is that there should be justice as far as these people are concerned. To that extent, I hope this act will improve matters; it has been a long time coming. I also hope to be able to participate in the committee hearings on this bill.
Bankruptcies involve far too much dirty laundry. We hear about thousands of people going bankrupt. Nonsense, they are not going bankrupt; there are some who have overextended themselves. They make conscious decisions. If they modify their spending policies and tighten up in certain areas, they may be able to ride out the storm. These people were not guaranteed a safe and smooth passage. They have to stand up to the realities of the decisions they took.
There is no doubt in my mind that there has been a lot of foolish spending and investment. People get carried away with the inflation psychology which is so prevalent today. The government is up to its neck in it. All the way along we have seen government proposals in legislation which accepts 10 and 12 per cent inflation as though it was going to happen. The proposal in the Judges Act was for an increase in salary in excess of 7 per cent, and this to be checked every three years. What is that but an acceptance of inflation?
One of the side benefits of the exceptionally high interest rates today will be to draw people away from this inflation psychosis so that they accept the idea that tomorrow is not necessarily the day when Santa Claus will come around with higher salaries. At the present time, they are hooked all the way through. In more than one government proposal we have seen indexing all the way along. That is an acceptance of the fact that inflation is as inevitable as the sun rising tomorrow somewhere in the world, and that is wrong.
However, having said that, it is no relief to those people who have made mistakes to say to them, "Tough luck, old boy, but you made the mistake, you have to get along with it and lump it." I hope that through this act ordinary debtors, the so-called
consumer debtors, commercial debtors and industrial concerns, will have flexible enough legislation for honesty and good will to be allowed to-

Mr. Speaker, I was moved to speak earlier when I listened to the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre), and I am moved even more so now as a result of listening to the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert).
When the latter hon. member was dealing with the priorities which are set in the bankruptcy legislation, I was reminded that income tax funds stand in a preferred position. As a matter of perhaps some little interest, when I was first elected to the House of Commons, the very first motion 1 put on the order paper was to the effect that the government, in collecting income taxes, should rank on an equal basis with other creditors. Believe it or not, I was successful in getting that particular motion through private members' hour and to the committee. At the committee I ran into a bit of opposition from, of all people, the financial critic of the New Democratic Party, who indicated that where other individuals had extended credit, they had made the conscious decision to extend that credit, and the government was really in no position to do so. On that basis, that member argued in favour of the proposition that the government should maintain its preference. I was not able to dissuade the committee, and by the time I got back to the committee again, the decision had pretty well been made.

subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY
speechtext:
1 want to commend the minister for being able to convince his cabinet colleagues that this particular piece of legislation should be brought forward. We have heard much rhetoric and there has been much wringing of hands about the suggestion that many other subjects should be discussed, given present interest rates, as well as the energy policy which is now being discussed and bills such as Bill C-48 and Bill C-57, but this particular bill is not brought forward in isolation. 1 understand there are some six different committees meeting this afternoon to discuss a whole series of subjects. Part of those discussions will involve the estimates of particular departments. If parliamentarians have an obligation, it is to go over those estimates with a fine-toothed comb and in that way act in the better interests of the constituents they serve. So I think the minister should be commended for being able to convince his cabinet colleagues that this was the time to bring this particular piece of important legislation forward, rather than be the butt of the wrath of some hon. members.
1 was somewhat appalled-that is the only word I can think of-when 1 listened to the hon. member for Calgary Centre condemning in a broad way trustees in bankruptcy. 1 do not know the trustees in bankruptcy with whom he has dealt, but I can say that it has been my experience that trustees are very dedicated individuals. In many instances they are members of the chartered accounting profession or the legal profession, and they perform a yeoman's service on behalf not only of the estates for which they are trustees in bankruptcy but also on behalf of a myriad of creditors, many of whom would not understand their rights if it were not for the trustees in
Bankruptcy
bankruptcy who quite often go the second mile to explain those rights to ordinary creditors. In many, many instances trustees have seen fit to keep operations going so that creditors or debtors would not be left without any money at all. As the hon. member for Edmonton West pointed out, quite often they have been able to arrange settlements whereby creditors get 70 cents, 80 cents or a certain amount on the dollar so that everyone has an opportunity to share in whatever assets are available.
To suggest that trustees milk estates until the last cent is gone so that they can discourage anybody from taking civil action I think does a disservice to trustees in bankruptcy who have served this country in a very admirable and conscientious fashion.
There will be bad ones, of course, in every profession, but I think the vast majority of trustees do a yeoman's service on behalf of the people who run into difficulty, who are endeavouring to secure at least some of their money back and who look to the trustee in bankruptcy as their last hope of collecting at least some cents on the dollar.
The hon. member for Calgary Centre indicated that the service people who came to Ottawa to speak to us last week put all the blame for their problems on the national energy policy. I must say that they were much more honest in their presentation than was the hon. member for Calgary Centre this afternoon. They indicated that they had seen not just our government but also the government of the Province of Alberta and the government of the province of Ontario. They were endeavouring not to be political, as the hon. member for Calgary Centre was in this instance. They were endeavouring to point out their difficulties. Some pointed out that in six months they would have to close up. They pointed out that many of them will have to go bankrupt unless an agreement is reached between the producing provinces and the federal government.

The hon. member from Edmonton West quoted a former principal of his who indicated that a bankruptcy was a natural and necessary tool or weapon, or perhaps opportunity is the best word, for people in business in the private sector in a capitalistic system. In this way people have extended credit to them, have taken that particular risk, sometimes securing the risk by floating debentures or mortgages or some other means, and in some instances they simply lent that money or performed the work, knowing they can protect themselves through the filing of mechanic's liens or things of that nature.
However, in every instance of a bankruptcy the individual or corporation has overextended itself, possibly by expanding too much, possibly by not rationalizing the machinery it has in its enterprise. There are many reasons for bankruptcy and I think Canadian society today does not look down upon bankruptcy in the same way it did many years ago. I think it is now accepted, and people who extend credit recognize that they are taking a risk and that it is their obligation, as the hon. member for Edmonton West said, to determine to what extent they should be prepared to advance goods or money or to allow someone to use a particular enterprise when the individual who needs it cannot pay cash for it on the spot.
So business decisions are made by people who extend credit, and people build up reputations for receiving credit, using that credit, making a profit and paying back the loan. In that way they set a pattern so that in the future when they enter other enterprises or develop their own, they will have built up a credit rating so that people will have some confidence in them and advance them credit.
It is always a tragic time when an individual or a corporation faces bankruptcy, and what we have to do at that particular time is at least to have legislation in place that will make it as easy as possible for people to overcome the trauma, to see if they can get some money out of the particular operation or to see if they can keep the operation going. Good trustees in bankruptcy will do that, if they can arrange a settlement that will be equitable for all concerned, and that is not only the trustee's responsibility but certainly is that of the individual or the corporation to the people who have extended credit.
All of us in this House are concerned about the ordinary wage earner, the individual who has no choice. He works for a particular corporation and is supposed to be receiving a salary, but he is put off so that at some point down the line he has to make a decision as to how long he is going to continue to work there in the knowledge that he may never receive the money. He has no particular priority. And I think the method the minister has endeavoured to put into this particular act is one that faces up to that particular problem. Maybe there is a better way and maybe someone will come forward at the committee stage with something that is better than what is provided for in the act, but I commend the minister for the fact that special attention has been given to the ordinary worker employed by a particular corporation who has not insisted upon payment of his wages in the interest of helping that corporation to continue.
There is one other area that I find particularly invidious, and that is the individual corporation that knows it is going bankrupt, continues to seek out credit and secures it, in some instances, from gullible people, and maybe we should not feel too sorry about them. Those companies convince people in construction, for example, not to file mechanic's liens because in doing so they will stop the flow of capital. Quite often a bank or a trust company will move in, advance more money than should be advanced and thus obtain a large advantage over all the ordinary creditors because these individuals have not filed mechanic's liens. When a construction subcontractor reaches a stage where he feels it is necessary, in order to protect his interests, to file a mechanic's lien, it is my view that unless he has something very solid from the contractor or the owner, he would be well advised to pull the plug, as it were, and call the bluff of the contractor to see if he can in fact proceed.
Now you cannot generalize on a subject like that, Mr. Speaker, because there are instances where an individual knows that if mechanic's liens are filed, the bank will not advance the money he needs to pay salaries and things of that nature. However, somehow we have to find a way to aid those who have been stuck as a result of companies and individuals

I hope that in the passage of this particular piece of legislation, as long as it is-and at 430 sections it reminds me to some extent of the Bank Act-we will have the same kind of co-operation. I hope we will have witnesses appearing before us who will have an idea about how we might protect the ordinary worker and if this is not the best system, whether there is a better system that could be implemented.
1 thank the House for its attention. I know that others want to speak, but I hope the bill will be referred to committee soon so we can have witnesses before us and give the bill a very close scrutiny in clause by clause reading. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

It is also interesting to realize that this basic legislation has been in the works in finalized form since 1975. I understand it has been introduced in the House by three different ministers at three different times over the past six years. In fact, it has taken the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) since last year to present a bill which is basically the same as the one presented by the Progressive Conservative party when we governed in the fall of 1979.
The lack of ingenuity on the part of the government is superseded only by its lack of speed. Rather than dwell on the intricacies of the legislation and the procedures for handling bankruptcies, I turn my attention to the provisions of the act which govern secured and unsecured creditors, especially with respect to the position of commission sales people and wage earners.
I am sure the government, in consultation with receivers and trustees, has done its best to streamline the procedures under the Bankruptcy Act. In any event, we can deal with those refinements in committee; we should not occupy the time of the House. Later I will comment upon the suggestion that the bankruptcies superintendent surveys trustees and receivers to determine the feasibility of establishing a funded plan to insure wage earners against loss of wages and other benefits caused by the bankruptcy of their employers.
I should like to deal with the question of preference. Traditionally preference has been given to wage earners vis-a-vis other unsecured creditors. The act proposes to continue that preference. I would suggest that we look very hard at the suggestion that wage earners should be granted priority over secured creditors for wages and commissions owed, as well as any deduction the employer has made for employee benefits, group insurance, income tax, etc.
Wage earners and commissioned salesmen are always hardest hit by a commercial bankruptcy. The loss of wages strikes at the pocketbook of the wage earner and his or her ability to feed and clothe a family and put a roof over their heads. These are not usually the sophisticated players in the business world. The sophisticated players are the banks, trust companies, finance companies, insurance companies and large businesses. They can sustain a loss; they know how to protect themselves. These are the people to whom salary cheques at the end of the week or every two weeks are all important. For that reason we should consider giving wage earners and commission sales people a priority over secured creditors. The hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Desmarais) was in the House a moment ago; he is also a chartered accountant.
At this point I would like to refer to the minutes of the Senate Standing Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce of Tuesday, June 3, 1980 in which Mr. Biddell, a well-respected trustee in bankruptcy, made some remarks with respect to the possible preference or security which could be given to wage earners. He spoke on behalf of the Institute of Chartered Accountants which presented a brief to the committee. He said:

-we think it is the secured lenders who should be required to contribute out of their security the amount required to pay the outstanding wages, because the employee's work has gone into enhancing the value of their security, for the most part, and the secured lender is the person best qualified to determine, not only his position but whether or not the company can continue to survive, what its chances are, and when, if it must, be terminated. This is the way commercial practice is going in Canada, and I think that this legislation should follow it.
The Institute of Chartered Accountants suggested that this security should be attached to current assets such as inventory and accounts receivable, not so much long-term fixed assets such as land and equipment. They suggested the money in cash which the trustee would have coming in from which to pay out secured claims of wage earners. This makes good sense; I hope the House and the committee consider it.
My next question concerns whether there should be any limit on the amount of salary and wages an employee may claim as either a secure or preferred creditor. I want to review this matter briefly and then make a special reference to real estate sales people on commission. The limit of $2,000 was presumably set with some principle in mind. I do not understand why there should be any limit on the wages and commissions payable which rank as either secured or preferred claims. It is the people who are working, whether they are commissioned sales persons or wage earners, who make the economic world go around. The very least we can do as members of Parliament is to protect their salaries, wages and commissions.
There may be any number of reasons why the amount owed to an employee at the time of bankruptcy may exceed $2,000. The employee may be a highly paid employee. The employee's pay dates may be monthly or at even longer intervals. If the employee is employed in the far north and only draws down his full pay at the end of a contract date, the amount owing could exceed $2,000. The employee may be on a bonus or incentive which normally results in large accruals of salaries or wages. In any event, I see no reason why there should be any limit on what is paid in a bankruptcy to an employee who is either a preferred or secured creditor.
Real estate sales persons are at a very distinct disadvantage under the Bankruptcy Act. First, the amount of commission on any one real estate transaction can very often exceed $2,000. Second, real estate sales persons do not receive their payment or commission until the transaction closes. This can mean a real estate sales person can work very hard in the month of May and sign up, for example, in five transactions which close in June, July and August. The work of the commission sales person has been done, the transaction is finished as far as they are concerned, but if anything happens to the financial stability of the broker during the period from the time the agent completes the offer to purchase to the time the commission is paid to the broker and thence to the sales person, the real estate sales person can find himself in difficulty. He can find that commissions receivable have been assigned to the bank or to other creditors and they are scooped before the real estate sales person is paid his commission.
If it is argued that the rationale for a $2,000 limit on wages and salaries is that an employee is expected to protect himself or herself, this does not ring true when we are talking about
commission sales people. They cannot do anything about the commissions owed to them. If one is working on the line, is paid every week, and does not get paid on one Friday or the following Friday, perhaps there is some responsibility on his part to say, "Hey, wait a minute, I will not work until they pay me." But real estate sales people and other commission sales people do not have that protection. They may not even be on the premises where the business takes place. Their part of the business may be to go out and make sales; they are not there to see day to day the financial stability of the company. I would suggest that we look at that, and if we maintain a preference system, we should consider whether $2,000 is high enough.

Mr. Speaker, when my time ran out at six o'clock I had just finished dealing with what I felt were inequities in placing a limit on the amount an employee could recover as a preferred claim on a bankruptcy. I would like to extend my comments one step further and talk about the provision in the legislation relating to a $500 limit on pension and health and welfare contributions. It seems to me that when an employer makes deductions from an employee's pay for group insurance benefits, health and welfare deductions and pension plans, the employer takes on a position of trust. The funds which are held by the employer for payment to the benefit of the employee are trust funds. The employee has no method of ascertaining that the funds have or have not been paid out on his or her behalf by the employer under the terms of the trust. No employee, no matter how diligent, can protect himself against an employer who, when faced with financial difficulties, decides to borrow from his employees in effect, and pay other creditors to the detriment of pension funds and health and welfare plans.
It is for that reason I wonder why there should be any limit on the trust moneys deducted by employers which are held, in effect, to be paid out under these plans for the benefit of the employees. It seems to me that the federal government has a responsibility under the terms of the Bankruptcy Act to enforce the terms of that trust.
The last thing I wish to deal with is the suggestion that the bankruptcy superintendent be empowered under the act to survey trustees and receivers to determine the feasibility of establishing a funded plan to insure wage earners against the loss of wages and other benefits caused by the bankruptcy of their employer. My first thought was, that in setting up such an investigative board, the Liberal party had run out of positions to which it could appoint Liberal politicians and
May 19, 1981

party faithful. I thought perhaps Maurice Strong had another idea. Then I went on to imagine the management consultants and economists who would be needed to produce such a study. I imagined the endless forms, the questionnaires and the paperwork which we would be loading on the Canadian business person who is trying to make a living. Then I started to contemplate who would be included in this favoured group of wage earners who will pay into a fund which will pay salaries when the employer goes bankrupt.
The first group of employees I thought about was federal government employees because, at the rate this government is running up deficits, they are prime candidates for bankruptcy. It can be seen that very soon civil servants should be paying into such a fund. I then went on to think about Crown corporations which would probably also be absolved from the payment of such premiums, despite the fact that organizations such as the CBC would never produce a profit, nor could they ever be expected to. I then wondered how an employer would explain to his employee a further deduction from his rapidly diminishing pay cheque. There would be a box on the pay slip which would read "bankruptcy deduction". I thought about my son who recently landed his first job. 1 could see him going to his employer and asking him what this bankruptcy deduction was all about. The employer would say that it was a fund from which my son would receive his wages when the employer went bankrupt. I do not see how this engenders any confidence in the system, to be deducting money from people's pay cheques right off the bat and telling them how they will be paid when their employer goes broke.
As I suggested earlier, it seems to me eminently more sensible to adopt the suggestion of the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants and give wage earners and commission sales people a priority over secured creditors from the remuneration or recovery on current assets.
I am also concerned as to how we would administer such a plan, the number of people that would be needed, and simply whether it makes sense; because although we are dealing with bankruptcies and we are definitely having more than we have had in the past, based on my 25 years of experience in business, 1 do not see that a fund and all the problems that go with such a fund are necessary to solve this problem. I think that if the Canadian government wants a survey, surely that questionnaire could have gone out to trustees and receivers without our asking for the approval of the House of Commons. With all of the things that the government does without our approval, one would think that surely a simple questionnaire such as this could be set up.
So, those are the remarks that I wanted to make on the Bankruptcy Act. We on this side of the House dearly hope that the government will get on with the legislation, that we can get it into committee, that we can solve this matter, and we will not have the hon. Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs bringing in this legislation once again.
