subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY
speechtext:
It is the people of this country who control the New Democratic Party, and not the major financial institutions of this country.
The Bankruptcy Act has some changes in it to clear up some of the problems with which we are faced, but not nearly enough. I really do believe that the small business people, the farmers, and especially the wage earners of this country, should be the ones to get the first crack at any money that is left over when a company becomes insolvent or has to declare bankruptcy.
The banks are the first ones to shout, though. They have everything secured. They keep in touch through political contributions and strong lobbying techniques that the average consumer does not have at his disposal. For example, early last year there were 50 employees from Lewis Motors (Ottawa) Ltd. right here in Ottawa. Did they all receive their money, or did Clarkson Gordon get its money first, or did the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce get its money first? And what was left over for the employees? I suspect there was very little left once the banks got through with them, because the banks, especially during high inflationary periods like this, get consumers, small businesses, especially farmers, into a situation of indebtedness with which they cannot cope. They have them secured and they end up with everything after the company or the farm has become insolvent or declared bankrupt. I do not think this is right.
The government actually introduced legislation in 1975 to clear up this situation but did not really pursue it. It was dropped at that time. Then the Senate pursued the matter. It felt that the banks should receive priority. I will quote Senator Hayden who summed it up by saying: "The committee took a strong view in relation to that proposal," talking about wage earner priority, "fearing that it would upset the whole business of commercial lending and commerical financing if secured creditors were deprived of their position." Deprived of what position? I wonder, when we are talking about the banks, these financial institutions.
About a month ago I saw an article in the Winnipeg Free Press headed, "Bank profits zoom". In the first quarter of 1980-81, the profits of the eight top chartered banks were up by $459.8 million. For that quarter, that means they were up 60.8 per cent over the previous year. Certainly they do not need that money as do some of the small individuals who are caught in the squeeze of high inflation and high interest rates which have been created by the Liberals in co-operation with the Conservatives before them, and who set the legislation to give priorities to the banking institutions to grease their political wheels. I think it is a disgrace.
I wonder how the interest rates affect Senator Hayden. I wonder how the interest rates affect some of the members of Parliament here. Certainly not as much as they affect the small consumers out in the constituencies which we are supposed to represent. It seems strange that it is the people who elect us, who put us here to run the country and set the rules of the country to govern in fairness and in good order, and yet we come down on the side of the banks and not the common,
everyday individuals out there who need our help, who do not have the resources at their fingertips to be able to manipulate the systems as well as the banks and larger corporations do. I think it is much more important to have the money put towards feeding a family than to put it into running a banking institution or financial institution which already has, as I have said, zooming profits, increased profits, year after year in this country.
The banks should be equally happy, I think, with the Tories as they are with the Liberals who are giving them this. I think that a good way of summing it up is that the Conservatives chopped the hole in the boat; but now that the captain is a Liberal, they are screaming because the water is getting in. It seems a very strange situation to me.
There are not many rich bankers in the constituency which I represent in northwestern Saskatchewan. The people there work very hard to make a living, as do people anywhere else in this country. They do not have the resources available to them that might be found in some of the larger centres, nor do they have some of the job opportunities that might be available there. A number of other members represent constituencies similar to mine where the people depend on small businesses which employ the vast number of people in this country. They depend on agriculture, and bankruptcies among small farms are increasing at an alarming rate. I understand that business bankruptcies have increased by close to 30 per cent. Some 697 businesses went bankrupt in March alone. That does not just refer to those small businesses where people have lost the work of a number of years or in some cases of their entire lifetime; it does not mean hardship only to them but to their employees, people who depend on those small businesses for the income with which they feed their families. This has a spin-off effect in the community.
The situation of the farmers is worsening, Mr. Speaker. In the first three months of 1981, farm bankruptcies increased 70 per cent over the same period last year. This does not take into consideration those farms where there was foreclosure or those farmers who had to sell out because they may have been too proud to declare bankruptcy and had to get out with some of their personal effects. These people lost everything. When we are passing legislation which relates to bankruptcy, I think it should help those people and not the banking institution.
I agree that the banks should have the ability to secure credit, but they should not have first call on it, Mr. Speaker. The people I have mentioned should have first call. When those people are paid off, there is usually something left but when banks and financial institutions have the first secured line of credit, there is very seldom anything left for the consumer or wage earner in the company involved.
I am quite concerned about what is happening in the area of agriculture. Bankruptcies may drive us into an agricultural or food crisis in this country within a few years, if they continue at the present rate. People are being driven out of cow-calf operations and out of grain farming because of the bad
May 19, 1981

economic conditions that face them. Perhaps the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) should turn his green cowboy hat in for a green poker visor because this government is playing poker, which is a high risk game, with the farmers, business people and wage earners of this country whose lives are adversely affected during these times.
We have a very serious problem in this country today. Rather than dealing with who should have priority when a company goes bankrupt, perhaps we should be dealing with legislation to keep businesses and farmers from falling into such a bad situation. In times of spiralling inflation, it is very difficult for them to carry on.
I should like to turn for a few moments to a matter which took place in the constituency of Battlefords-Meadow Lake. A short time ago, 27 farmers in northwestern Saskatchewan purchased some very expensive farm equipment from an implement dealer in North Battleford. The implement dealer agreed that the farmers would put down a small amount and pay the rest after a set period of time. Unfortunately, he ran into some financial problems and did not pass on all the money paid to him for the machinery purchased by the farmers. Instead, he saw it as a cheap source of interim financing that he could use to get his business back on a good footing, at which time he would pay the money back. He never passed the money along to the trust company which held the notes for the cost of the equipment, however, and his business got into a worse situation. His indebtedness spiralled and he found himself unable to honour his commitments to business. Rather than declare bankruptcy, he sold the business to another implement dealer. This was not really a case of bankruptcy, but if he had declared bankruptcy the outcome would have been the same.
When he sold the business, the trust company became interested in his financial situation. It wanted its money for the equipment that had been sold to the 27 farmers in the Batt-lefords area. The man who owned the company said, "I am sorry, I cannot pay you." He signed a promissory note to the trust company saying, "Yes, I owe you this sum of money", which actually amounted to $246,694.88. He said, "Yes, I owe this, but I cannot pay it." He sold a car he owned and gave that money to the trust company. He sold a house he owned and gave that money to the trust company. The courts were not even able to find out what had happened to the money that had come in when he sold his business. So he was unable to pay this almost quarter of a million dollars to the trust company which said, "We want our money." The implement dealer said, "I cannot pay it." The trust company said, "Well, we want the equipment." The implement dealer said, "I cannot give it to you. The farmers have it." The trust company went to the farmers and tried to seize the equipment, which they needed to carry on their farming operations. As far as the farmers were concerned, they had already paid for their equipment, but the trust company still wanted it.
One of the farmers said, "Lookit, you can't have my equipment. I need it to carry on farming and I need to farm in order to feed my family and pay my taxes to this great family." He
Bankruptcy
took the trust company to court. The final court decision was that the farmer had to pay for the equipment again. The farmer had to pay the trust company twice! Twice for the same equipment! That is wrong, Mr. Speaker.
There are several things wrong with this situation, some of which relate to federal legislation and some to provincial legislation. Part of the problem with the provincial legislation concerns the bonding of implement dealers. The provincial government of Saskatchewan has been very responsive and is introducing legislation this session to ensure that such a situation will not occur in that province again. The federal government should be doing something about it as well. No one should have to pay twice for the same material. The farmers paid in good faith to an implement dealer who unscrupulously used the money for his own benefit to try to put his company back on a sound footing. He thought of it as low interest money and did not pass it along to the trust company. That should not be allowed to happen.
The same situation would have held true if he had declared bankruptcy. The courts would still have ruled in favour of the trust company which wanted its money-which seized the collateral or asked for double payment.
It is situations such as the one I have outlined which point out that wage earners and the people of this country who are least able to afford the loss when a bankruptcy occurs should have first recourse against the assets, not the trust company.
Can you imagine what it does to 27 farming families in one area who in some cases have to pay as much as $30,000 or more for the same piece of equipment, and to pay for it twice? In times of inflation, just as now when equipment is already overpriced, when interest rates are out of sight, when fuel prices are creating hardship and adding to the inflationary spiral, I say it is wrong to give these companies first priority over those funds and to turn private individuals out into the cold. That is not being a very responsive government. I do not think the government appreciates what some of the people have to put up with in constituencies outside of Ottawa.
Ottawa is not the real world, Mr. Speaker. 1 am sure you are aware of that, even though your constituency is in Ottawa. Ottawa is removed from the real world. I think some members of Parliament, especially Liberal members of Parliament, should be keeping in closer touch with their constituents and listening to what they say when it comes to who should have priority in cases of bankruptcy. Almost every lobby and organized group, outside of Ottawa and the banking and financial institutions, recommend that it is the individual, the wage earner and the small business person who should have first chance at recovery of assets in cases of bankruptcy.
We should examine what other countries do, instead of just listening to what the banks have to say. For example, the Swedish government has a wage guarantee law. In this respect employers pay into a fund. I do not know that anyone from the Liberal government has looked into that aspect to see if it is feasible in Canada. It sounds good to me. But as a member of

May 19, 1981
Bankruptcy
Parliament I certainly do not have the resources or the research staff to look into something like this. The government should do such research when it is introducing a bill like this.
In France the government helps employees of a bankrupt firm to find work. The government guarantees pay for a year if those employees cannot find work. Why does Canada not think about doing that? Does the federal government not have control of the economy? Have we lost total control? Do we not care any more? It seems that we are in a firefighting situation most of the time. We react to a crisis situation, instead of planning ahead. We should plan an industrial strategy. More important, we should plan an economic policy to ensure that hardships, which certainly do and will occur over time, are spread over as large a base of the population as possible. This hardship should be spread around, especially on those with the economic resources, such as financial institutions. They should absorb some of that hardship, instead of forcing some farmers into a bankruptcy or into having to pay twice for equipment that they could hardly afford in the first place.
Many members of Parliament, especially Liberal members, because they are the ones who are introducing this bill, have to hide their heads in the sand and choke back the injustice which is being created by legislation like this being put into place. They have to hold their noses to put it through because it reeks of paying the piper and calling the tune. I am referring to the money given to the old line political parties by the financial institutions of this country. It is almost unbelievable that something like that could happen in Canada at a time when we are trying to draw up a Constitution to govern the country in fairness and equality for all people. Much of the legislation we bring in is firefighting legislation. It is reactive legislation. It is reactive to the heaviest pressure groups, which include the banks. The banks pressure individual members of Parliament to introduce legislation which will be advantageous to the banks. The banks grease the wheel by giving contributions to the old line political parties. That is a terrible way to set laws in this country. If the same thing is happening with respect to our Constitution, then I think this country is in real trouble. We should be looking at the very base by which we govern ourselves. We should be listening to the people from firms such as Lewis Motors. We should be listening to the farmers who bought implements from dealers who handle their funds unscrupulously. We should listen to the way some of these people have been treated by the unjust laws that we have created in this chamber.
I can be even more critical of the Senate which has spearheaded this bill. Senator Hayden has argued that it will upset the financial balance of this country if the first line of retrieval of assets is given to employees or to individuals and not to the financial institutions. The Senate is even more removed from the real world than some members of Parliament. I wonder how long it has been since any senator has had to deal on credit? I am sure some of them deal with credit because many of them are in business. Business evolves around credit. Senators, however, have financial reserves so they do not have to depend for their very living on credit, as many of the people
out in the work place do, out on the small farms and in small business. Some of these rights should be taken away from the Senate and maybe some of the senators would declare bankruptcy from time to time. They would know what it feels like to be down and out bankrupt. They are not bankrupt in terms of financial assets, but they are certainly bankrupt in terms of the ideas and the morals they have to bring forward and recommend legislation such as this which gives the first crack at bankrupty assets to the financial institutions of this country.
If this bill cannot be changed to protect those people who need to be protected most, I feel somewhat ashamed. I would never be able to give my support to a piece of legislation such as this which does not protect the people we are here to represent.

subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate briefly in this important debate, I gave quite a bit of thought to the word bankruptcy. Most of us in this chamber have run across people who are morally bankrupt. I am not pointing my finger particularly at any hon. members on the government side of the House at this time. We politicians may even accuse each other of being intellectually bankrupt from time to time.
Originally, the word bankrupt was only applied to fraudulent persons. The first bankruptcy act in Great Britain was directed against such "persons as do make bankrupt." These people were defined as those:
-who craftily obtaining unto their hands great substance of other men's goods do suddenly flee to parts unknown or keep to their houses not minding to pay or restore to any of their creditors their debts and duties.

subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY
speechtext: That is Allan MacEachen.

subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY
speechtext:
Clearly and thankfully the interpretation of the word "bankrupt" has become somewhat more lenient since the days of Henry VIII, although those responsible for the economic situation that we are in, and which is leading to so many bankruptcies, have been known to flee to parts unknown. Again, no names will be mentioned.
It is when you examine the word "bankruptcy" as an individual, as a small businessman, that its definition makes it the most fearsome word imaginable when it comes to a person's economic well-being, not to mention self-esteem. Bankruptcy is indeed a hurtful, demoralizing thing. This is how Funk and Wagnall's Standard Encyclopedic Dictionary defines bankruptcy:
1.	Law-One who is judicially declared insolvent, his property being administered for and distributed among his creditors, under a bankruptcy law.
2.	Any person unable to pay his debts, or without resources.
3.	One ruined and unproductive in some way.
The adjective "bankruptcy" is:
1.	Subject to the conditions of a bankruptcy law; insolvent.
2.	Destitute; lacking.
Some of the previous speakers in this debate dealt with the technical and the political aspects of this bankruptcy legisla-
May 19, 1981

tion. Let me take a more personal people view of this issue. As a small businessman, and especially the small business I was operating before 1 entered politics, the spectre of bankruptcy was always there. Mine was an innovation in the electronic communications business and certainly in the parliamentary Press Gallery. It was to provide coverage of Parliament to some 20 individual television stations across Canada, feeding them news film clips of their local MPs on an almost daily basis.
While the idea was a sound journalistic principle and filled a real gap before broadcasting entered this House of Commons, such a venture require many thousands of dollars of capital investment in terms of camera equipment, film stock and, above all, people. During my ten years of operating the company, I employed or contracted 12 to 15 men and women, reporters and cameramen alike, with a total staff of seven people at one time during peak periods.
That may not sound like a very big operation when compared to other businesses such as farms and smaller industrial operations, but I can tell you about the vagaries of the broadcasting industry, about the unpredictability of the news business and, most certainly, about the uncertainties of the economy. Interest rates then were 9 to 10 per cent, one half of what they are now, but they were high. I can you tell especially about the exceptionally fine talents of the upwardly mobile young men and women who gained experience in my small company to move on, inevitably and justifiably, to larger and more lucrative employment in regional and national networks. All of these factors made life in my small business at best uncertain. I am proud of those former employees who used my company as a training ground. Several are major names today in the field of electronic journalism.
The turnover of reporters and technical personnel, and the ever-present fuse that was to lead to the explosion in technology in the news business-especially the conversion from film to videotape tranmission-along with increasing competition from the network giants, made it imperative that my accountant and I keep looking over our left shoulders to the very real probability of being forced out of business. For me, such a prospect of increasing corporate control could have meant that awesome possibility of bankruptcy.
Fortunately, thanks to the diligence of my company secretary-treasurer, who, by staggering coincidence, happens to be my wife, and thanks also to the good people of Hamilton-Wentworth, my little company survived. That is as close as I ever want to come to being, as the definition says, "without resources" or "one ruined and unproductive in some way".
It is also a reason that I can understand, and sympathize with, the agony that so many small businesses, some a lot bigger, some considerably smaller than mine, must endure under the present economy. I understand the helplessness these good, entrepreneurial Canadians must feel as they are forced to declare bankruptcy, largely because, as was pointed out many times today, of unconscionably high interest rates and an increasing lack of sensitivity to free enterprise initiatives in this country.
Bankruptcy
Let me point out as an aside, but not entirely unrelated to the question of bankruptcy, that it is an insidious thing that is creeping into our society where government is permitting its own government operations to take over small business. There have been more and more takeovers. I think it can be safely said that the only businesses that are sure to survive in this country are owned by the government and supported by tax dollars.
Earlier today the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) asked that members participating in this debate restrict their discussion to legal matters and not get into economics. That is like saying that if you go to Florida these days, you should ignore the sinkholes and just count the number of houses and trees which tumble into them. It is little wonder that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs does not want to discuss the economy. I must point out to the minister that the number of business bankruptcies were up in the first quarter of 1981 to 2,044, compared to 1,706 in the first quarter of 1980.

subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY
speechtext:
That is increased
productivity.

subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY
speechtext:
The total number of bankruptcies in 1980 was 6,595. Surely we can expect this number to increase in 1981 in light of this government's economic policies, or lack of them.
I want to address a very important issue which several of my colleagues signalled should be discussed when dealing with this legislation. The proposed legislation before us, Bill C-12, grants the first claim on the assets of a bankrupt firm to the secured creditors. These secured creditors take precedence over the wage earners who have lost their jobs through the bankruptcy. This bill maintains the same priority on the claims of wage earners as does the present act.
This aspect of the bill is one which greatly affects many of my people and indeed, many of all our constituents. In these days of more and more bankruptcies, it is a problem we will undoubtedly be hearing more about.
When a company, whether it be large or small, goes bankrupt, the claims of the secured creditor to the firm's assets are to be fulfilled first. If there are any assets left after these claims, then Bill C-12 makes provisions for the wages and commissions of the employees, but only after the secured claims have been dealt with.
Members of this House know that there will be very little, if anything, left to pay the wage earners of the company. The preferred credit status as outlined in section 265(4)(d) of the act almost ensures this inequity. This section sets a maximum of $2,000 in unpaid wages, and an additional $500 for pension plan and other employee benefits. As other speakers have pointed out, there is no question that these provisions must be given careful review by the committee which studies this bill.
I would like to comment on two aspects of this section. It would appear that the average wage earner, should he not be receiving his salary, or choosing not to draw it in the hopes

May 19, 1981
Bankruptcy
that the firm will find a way out of its financial crisis, will be severely penalized for not collecting or demanding his or her wages immediately. There is no incentive for the wage earner to attempt to help the firm through a difficult period.
I would also point out that the maximum amount of wages as outlined in section 265(4)(e) will be quickly outdated in these days of increasing inflation.
The Senate Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce, studying Bill C-12, received a great number of representations concerning the protection of employees whose employer has gone bankrupt. This committee reported that under Bill C-12, if there are sufficient assets of the bankrupt firm, then the wage earners will not be paid. I quote:
Your committee is of the opinion that this result is unsatisfactory.
They go on to list the three alternative solutions to remedy this problem. This can be found at pages 16:16 and 16:17 of the Senate banking, trade and commerce committee minutes:
1.	The granting to the wage earner of a statutory priority for arrears of wages that would rank in priority to the claims of all secured creditors.
That is called super priority.
2.	The granting to the wage earner of a statutory priority for arrears of wages that would rank in priority to the claims of the secured creditors holding security on the current assets of the bankrupt.
That is modified priority.
Such current assets would consist of cash, temporary investments, inventory and receivables provided that such priority would only extend over receivables which have been created by the supply of goods or services.
3.	The creation of a Wage Earners Protection Fund out of which the claims of employees for unpaid wages would be paid immediately after a bankruptcy has occurred.
Each of these alternatives must be considered in order to determine whether the following objectives are achieved:
A.	Certainty of payment to the wage earner.
B.	Promptness of payment to the wage earner.
C.	Ease and simplicity of administration.
D.	Maintenance of the ability of a borrower to obtain financing for his
business operations.
The committee felt that only the establishment of a wage earners' protection fund would fully protect wage earners in a bankruptcy. The committee suggested that this wage earners' protection fund be financed, as recommended by the Senate committee, by monthly contributions from all employers in the nation. This would mean a nominal amount paid per employee. It would only be required from employers with more than six employees. Technically, at one point during my company's operations that would have applied to me if this provision had been in effect. If an employer went bankrupt, the employee would be entitled to his claim for wages paid out of the fund, whether or not the employer was required to make contributions to the fund. The committee recommended that this type of fund be established in Canada to protect the interests of the wage earner.
1 find a great number of problems with a wage earners' protection fund, but I do believe it deserves serious study. Mind you, any fund would have to be controlled more tightly
than anything we have seen so far. We do not need another Unemployment Insurance Commission. Indeed, if the wild abuses of the UIC were even remotely approached, I would be the first to be scared off this idea of a wage earners' protection fund.
However, I would like to commend the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs for establishing a committee to study wage protection of some kind under the guidance of Mr. Raymond Landry. It is both an admission of the shortcomings of the bill as well as a concern that wage earners should be taken care of. I will be particularly interested in hearing representations and reading the testimony of those appearing before the committee as to why a wage earners' protection fund should be put in place as opposed to the position put forward by the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants, which zeroed right in on the fact that the administrative problem in collecting wage funds would be a very great one indeed. Representatives of the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants, appearing before the same Senate Standing Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce, said the following:
-we think it is the secured lenders who should be required to contribute out of their security the amount required to pay the outstanding wages, because the employee's work has gone into enhancing the value of their security, for the most part, and the secured lender is the person best qualified to determine, not only his position but whether or not the company can continue to survive, what its chances are, and when, if it must, be terminated.
There are two distinct and differing points of view, but the important point I want to leave with the House tonight is that the protection of the wage earner should be considered and studied by the kind of committee the minister has recommended.
Let me underline two points which previous speakers touched on this afternoon. The first one is somewhat political. This indeed may be housekeeping legislation, but in the context of today's economy it does seem like band-aid stuff. The government takes advantage of the absence of its two architects of Canada's economic illnesses, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), neither of whom have ever had to meet a mortgage payment or face a bankruptcy in their lives, and brings on this debate on bankruptcy legislation after the fact, after the damage has been done to businesses and to individuals because of the economic policies of this government.
That being said, as has also been pointed out, there are many technical provisions in this proposed legislation which are well drafted, well merited and deserve the support of all sides of the House. I do hope that when all 420 clauses of this bankruptcy and insolvency legislation are examined in committee, hon. members once again will safeguard the rights of employees more than they are safeguarded now. Speaking personally, I want to see some action taken to protect those who are abused by sharp operators who intentionally set up or take over a company and then bleed it to death and escape scot-free, *f hon. members will pardon the expression. My colleagues and I will be watching the progress of this bill through the committee with interest on behalf of many thou-
May 19, 1981

sands of Canadians who face the spectre of that awful word "bankruptcy".

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak about Bill C-12, respecting bankruptcy and insolvency, I am aware, of course, that there has been a great deal of consultation already in relation to its 420 clauses since its predecessor was first introduced way back in 1975. It is a pretty hefty document and one which indeed merits much consultation and study. However, in looking at the minister's press release which came out when the bankruptcy bill was first tabled in the House of Commons back on April 16, 1980, I note that in the press release it is stated, and I quote:
Mr. Ouellet added that once the bill is enacted, it will establish a comprehensive, workable and, above all, a fair bankruptcy system.
The bankruptcy system this bill seeks to establish may be fair, but there is nothing fair about the way that hundreds of small businessmen and farmers and individuals are being forced into bankruptcy by high interest rates and the high interest rate policy of this government. I look again at the figures, which came to my attention just recently, with regard to bankruptcies in the first quarter of this year. In the first quarter of 1981, there were 75 farm bankruptcies compared with 44 in the first quarter of 1980. There were some 2,044 business bankruptcies in the first quarter of 1981, compared with 1,706 in the first quarter of 1980.
With regard to personal bankruptcies, there were 6,152 in the first quarter of 1981 compared with 5,238 in the first quarter of 1980. In every case-farm bankruptcies, business bankruptcies and personal bankruptcies-the number is up very considerably.
These bankruptcies are not confined to any one sector or any one region of the country. By looking through recent press headlines, we can tell that bankruptcies are spread out across the country and that people are suffering because of bankruptcy everywhere. The headline in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of April 17 says "Bankruptcy... and the consumer". The headline in the Charlottetown Guardian of March 9 was "Bankruptcies increase". The headline in the Winnipeg Free Press of March 20 was "Bankruptcy liabilities highest in ten years". The headline in The Globe and Mail of March 7 is this: "Alarming rise in bankruptcies viewed as only tip of iceberg". Finally, in the London Free Press of April 23 of this year the headline was: "Farm bankruptcies rise, interest rates blamed". And from today's edition of the Kingston Whig Standard, a newspaper in my own constituency, this is the reaction of small businessmen who are having to face the increasing fear of bankruptcy. It reads as follows:
If there's one thing all business people agree on it's that the high interest situation can't go on indefinitely. They can survive in the shorter term; it's the longer term they fear.
Many businesses are running on such narrow margins that they're only paying the interest on their loans.
Bankruptcy
This bodes ill for the future. A business with nothing left over to plough back into the operation will, in a few years, find it has no capital when the need comes to refurbish or to expand.
And one of the businessmen in my constituency says this:
I've never in my life in 30 years in this business seen anything so ridiculous as what we're going through right now.
That is the way that Mac Amey, an American Motors dealer, sums it up. He claims that unless the federal government puts a ceiling on interest rates for small businesses and farmers, he can see 50 per cent of the people out of business within a few years. He also says:
High interest rates and low returns are deterring people from putting their personal money into business.
Nobody, as he puts it, "is going to put his money into a dead horse." Eric Bolton, who runs Boyd and Corkey Furniture and Appliances expresses the same view. He says:
Eventually this (high interest rates) will put us out of business ... You can only find so many corners to cut and then eventually you're at the end of the road.
Now, that is an article which appeared in tonight's edition of the Kingston Whig Standard, and in all of these newspapers all across the country we are reminded over and over again of the interrelationship between bankruptcy and high interest rates. I was interested, Mr. Speaker, in a quotation from The Financial Post of last week in a front page article which reads as follows:
The breathtaking switchabouts in interest rates over recent months, have left so many forecasters beached with wildly wrong predictions, and created so much confusion, that the public is increasingly wary of assertions from economic soothsayers ...
There is indeed wariness, Mr. Speaker, indeed suspicion on the part of the public about the soothsayers who sit on the government benches. The government has been all wrong in its projection in the last budget and ever since, and Canadians are not only wary of what they are doing, they are getting very weary of it as well.
The economic situation in the country, Sir, is chaotic. Interest rates are at an all time high, just under 19 per cent as of today. Rates being charged by the chartered banks are about 20 per cent, and bankruptcies are at an all time high. The government's own Federal Business Development Bank is charging 22 per cent on its loans; inflation is running at just under 13 per cent. Almost one million people are unemployed, no matter how the government boasts of its back-to-work record. We now have to deal with the worst economic situation that Canada has faced in 50 years. But is that, Sir, what the present cabinet ministers said while they sat in opposition? Oh, no, it was then that they boasted that they could cure all the ills of the country. In the Toronto Star of February 10, 1980, the then leader of the opposition, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), was quoted as follows:
I would want to manage the economy in such a way that interest rates would in fact come down ... because the economy would be administered in a sounder way.
Well, whatever he may have wanted, Sir, he certainly has not been able to manage it. And then there was the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) quoted in The Toronto

May 19, 1981
Bankruptcy
Sun of February 4, 1980, and I see him standing just outside the curtains and he may remember this, as having said:
It is my belief we can manage the economy in a way that would allow us to have lower interest rates than we have now and I think we can have greater independence in interest rate policy.
I don't think that allowing the dollar to have some downward adjustment-
I hope the minister is listening.
-would do as much harm to our economy, as our present high level of interest rates.
I wonder if the minister remembers that. I wish he had carried that message to his Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen). And again the same minister speaking in the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs on October 30, 1979 said this to the then minister of finance:
Mr. Minister-your high interest rate policy-
It was a lot lower than the interest rate is at the present time, but he said:
-will put housing beyond the reach of most middle and lower-income Canadians. It will hurt small business, which depends on bank borrowing to operate. It will hurt farmers, who have the same dependency on bank borrowing and will add, therefore, to the cost of food.
I am sure we can all say amen to that, and I wish the minister were saying those words today. But what he was saying and what others were saying at that time when they were in opposition, Sir, was that a high interest rate policy will lead to bankruptcies all across the country, personal, small business and farm bankruptcies.
Yes, the Liberal opposition was then concerned about high interest rates which were running at about 12 per cent, 13 per cent, 14 per cent and how those rates would lead to an increasing number of bankruptcies. Flowever, once back in office their concern vanished. They could not care less about the root causes of bankruptcies, all they are concerned about is the way in which they were handled. In opposition the Liberal spokesmen promised goods that they could not deliver and they knew they could not deliver, and now they are beginning to be caught out and people are beginning to vent their anger against what the government has done, because you see, Sir, people really do not like being cheated and outsmarted and duped, and eventually made to pay the price.
The government, and particularly the Minister of Finance who some would say has led a charmed political life, is now under attack and he does not like it, and so the government stutters and stumbles and staggers its way through a barrage of criticism of its own making. Yes, they weave and they bob and they duck and they blame the situation on everybody but themselves. We have the minister saying that he cannot control our high interest rates because the American rates are too high. He says he cannot make a dent in inflation because people's expectations are too high. It is the Minister of Finance who is bankrupt as far as any ideas of improving this situation are concerned, and so he turns to hon. members on the other side of the House and pleads with them: Tell me what to do. He forgets that he is the Minister of Finance and that the present Liberal cabinet while in opposition made the fatuous
promise that if the Liberal party were re-elected they would know exactly what do do.
Well, these days, Sir, safely out of sight in the inner sanctum of their departmental buildings, remote from real life, they move from consideration of higher interest rates to consideration of wage and price controls or to a tax based incomes policy. You can do that sort of thing if you are safely secluded in the penthouse of Place Bell Canada, but it shows that the government is bankrupt of ideas, of dollars and of any sense of responsibility.
However, in their distress they cry out for ideas. I offered one to the Minister of Finance the other day, that he set up a human misery index, something like the consumer price index but one which he can read daily so he will be aware of the hardship that he and the Liberal government are causing people. He will not be able to read that index on a beach in Hawaii, in Kuwait or even in Gabon where he is at the present time, but surely he can read it if he goes across the country and talks to small businessmen, farmers, individuals and people on fixed incomes. He will find out then what the human misery index is all about.
The other day we on this side were accused of pretending to be sympathetic to the plight of these people. In the situation which now confronts us, there is certainly no need to pretend. The suffering is there, the hardship is there, the uncertainty and the insecurity are there. With them there is a growing feeling that somehow the economic situation is running completely out of control. Many, many Canadians are beginning to consider their own situations as hopeless.
If that is lurid language, as the Minister of Finance said the other day, let me give him and the government an example. I started to elaborate on this the other night when the clock reached 10 p.m. Last weekend I received a call to visit and talk with two of my friends. They are a husband and wife team who are in the hotel business. I have known them for 15 years. I know how hard-working they are. I know how committed they are to providing their customers with the very best service they can possibly offer. Because of the way they have run their business, it has always been well patronized. Some two years ago they decided to restore their building to its original lines and decor, to go back to the time when it was First built in Kingston 150 years ago. It is a big undertaking, but it is one which will enhance the historical reputation of Kingston.
The decision to restore their building certainly was not taken lightly. They did so after much thought and consultation with their banker, architects and friends. When I went over to see them that afternoon, I found them deep in despondency. I knew the situation was very serious for them. They told me that two years ago they borrowed some $650,000 in order to carry out this restoration. At that time they were paying 12 per cent interest on it. After the latest increase in the government's bank rate, they are now paying 21 per cent; an interest payment of some $3,000 per week.
May 19, 1981

What is so heart-breaking about their case is that they are working harder than ever and they are taking in more money than ever before, but when they put their weekly deposit into the bank, $3,000 is immediately grabbed off to pay interest rates. They have only enough left over to meet the salaries of their staff. Their cheques for supplies are being turned back. Their payment of $5,000 to Revenue Canada was returned the other day marked "NSF". To add insult to injury, government officials had slapped a $300 penalty charge on that cheque for non-payment. The reason they could not pay it in the first place was because of that same government's high interest rates.
This couple has always done everything on their own, as have so many other small businessmen across the country who make up the very backbone of our economy, and they end up being forced into bankruptcy. They applied for a small business development bond some five months ago, and it still has not been processed. So, they have to continue paying high interest rates week after week after week. Now they find themselves on the verge of despair, not knowing when they will be forced out of business, not knowing how to break the news to their 40 employees that they may no longer have jobs. That couple is but one facing a very bleak future.
I can cite another example of a small businessman who combines running a small business with a farm operation. His small business is in the farm industry sector which means he must stock up in inventory of farm machinery. As everyone knows, he must borrow against that inventory. That is normal, that is usual. But also, as most people know, the farm machinery business is slow. Its pace has become very slow. Anyone who has been following the trials and tribulations of Massey-Ferguson is aware of that, but the difference between Massey-Ferguson and the farmers and small businessmen in this country is that the government steps in to help out Massey-Ferguson massively. But, there is no help for the farmer or small businessman caught in the same situation. This man of whom I am speaking is now liable to have all or part of his farm seized to pay for the farm machinery loan. This farm has been in his family for generations. He too is feeling an overwhelming sense of despair and hopelessness. He would have a high rating on the human misery index.
What am I supposed to tell these people when they come to me for advice. Am I supposed to tell them to hold on for a few more weeks or months, absorb the increase? With what? Am I supposed to tell them what the Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. Evans) told the House last week? He said:
The fundamental factor involved in this high interest rate condition is the transition through which we are going toward a more appropriate monetary policy for a lower inflation rate in the future.
In that barrage of words which add up to nothing what am I to tell my constituents who are losing their businesses and family farms? That kind of thing just does not register on the human misery index; that kind of gobbledygook just does not wash with Canadians who are suffering. I challenge the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance to use that line
Bankruptcy
on any one of his constituents to see if it calms their fears about the future.
Fear for the future is very real among Canadians, especially those who are the hardest hit by the interest rate-inflation spiral in which we are now. As high interest rates fuel inflation instead of bringing it down, as the minister projected, it becomes more and more difficult for those on fixed and low incomes to keep food on the table.
The problem will get worse before it gets better. Even the governor of the Bank of Canada has acknowledged things will only get worse, when he said last week that the disease the country has contracted is not just a high inflation but escalating inflation. Does the government not realize what escalating inflation really means, apart from adding decimal points to our cost of living figures? Does the minister not realize what it means when prices for essential goods and essential foods have skyrocketed since interest rates started spiralling? I have mentioned before how basic food staples have gone up and up and up in the last year. All of these items, as they go up, add to a grocery bill which more and more people cannot afford. Many of them are being forced into personal bankruptcy because of the high interest rates. So we are caught in a vicious circle with inflation fueling high interest rates and, in turn, high interest rates fueling inflation. As the circle tightens, the small businessman and the consumer are strangled in the middle. The number of bankruptcies might be high now but I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the number will grow before it diminishes if the government's present policies continue.
We need good bankruptcy laws; but more than that we need to stop the cause of bankruptcy. More than anything else we need preventive medicine, which means an interest rate policy that does not crush the small businessman before he has a chance to carry out his business. If we do not do something to attack the root of the problem, then this bill which we are considering will end up being the same kind of after-the-fact band-aid measure which the Liberal government has had to use over and over again to try to patch up a mess of its own creation. Bankruptcies are there because they have a cause. In Canada, many of these bankruptcies are being, and will continue to be, caused by the irresponsible monetary and fiscal policies of the government.

subtopic: BANKRUPTCY ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKRUPTCY AND INSOLVENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to carry along on the basis of the principle and philosophy behind bankruptcy legislation, following the closing remarks of the hon. member for Kingston and the islands (Miss MacDonald). I think all members of this House recognize that legislation covering bankruptcy is a federal measure which has been in need of reform for at least 15 years or longer. Great efforts have been made in the House, as well as in the other place, to come to a practical way of handling this necessary business adjustment, both in the personal profits of people as well as commercial operations. But we should also keep in mind, with regard to the question of debt, that the

May 19, 1981
Bankruptcy
provinces have a long experience in this type of matter. I would like to mention a couple of items which need no explanation. They are well understood.
I am talking about the mechanic's lien act, in which the working man always receives first right in the case of any kind of debt not paid. This applies in all the western provinces. I am talking about threshermen's liens, which in the east are called subcontractors' liens, where the worker has preference over federal legislation and everyone else, including banks. Naturally, as I look at this bill, I search for this same kind of protection. There has been some forward motion in this regard, but the man who produces the wealth, the labouring man and the subcontractor, is still not placed in the highest priority position, where he should be.
1 hope that in committee there will be some amendments which give equality of right to the working man who produces the wealth, as well as to the subcontractor who organizes the various streams of operations which go into the production of goods. I will not spend a great deal of time on this aspect, since it is indicative of the fact that this legislation is necessary. It can be improved. This is where the common sense and experience of members of Parliament close to their constituents can be very helpful.
I would like to go on to the history of one incident which struck me many years ago. We have had great collapses in parts of Canada on previous occasions. There is no one in this House who remembers the collapse of 1919 when farmers simply went bankrupt holus-bolus, banks closed down and refused to give credit to farmers because of the disastrous drop in prices after the Kaiser war. The second major experience which we have had in our history on this matter of credit delinquency occurred in the 1930s. Once again Parliament came through with fairly sensible legislation, the 1933 Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. This was a hallmark in social philosophy applied to a financial situation. It is no wonder that this was legislation drafted by westerners, but it was accepted by Parliament. Under the legislation, creditors and debtors would sit down with a government representative working under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act and look at the potential and real value of a farm. The first step was to scale down the debts to that potential, making it possible, with the expected hypothetical earnings, for that farmer to continue farming without going into bankruptcy. That legislation, which was extremely acceptable and well received by everyone, including the banks, enabled them to collect the money owed by the farmer and allowed the farmer to hang on to his farm. As far as the banks were concerned, it saved them cutting of their noses to spite their faces.
The second measure taken by Parliament was in 1934 when amendments were passed to the farm loans legislation which accompanied the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. In some cases the farmer could borrow money at low rates of interest, which were then the economic rates, to pay off certain types of debtors who could not, for their human and social interests, take their money over long extended periods. I mention these two items to remind the House that this situation, which was so vividly described by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands is not a new phenomenon. Past parliaments have coped with these problems in a practical and sensible way. Not everything was solved, but at least the tremendously dangerous effects that we all foresee with this high interest rate policy were cushioned.
I will not make my remarks purely partisan. I will try to be constructive in putting forward some proposals which I think are within the structure of the government to meet and which, at the same time, will not entail any subsidy by the government from the people it is trying to help. Let us learn from the experience of previous parliaments which had to grapple with a similar situation. As we know today from quantitative analysis, in heavily capitalized industries-and many of our industries fall within that category-the biggest single cost over an extended period of time is the amount of money which goes to interest. These are called capital intensive industries. For the very large industries with long pay-outs, 75 per cent of the total costs are due to capital repayments and interest charges. The average figure for the oil industry in Alberta from 1922 until 1957 was 75 per cent. Oil prices were low at that time, as were costs, and the industries were still able to make out because even at $1.50 at the wellhead, the costs of actual out-of-pocket money were only about 25 cents per barrel. The interest costs were around a dollar. The industry survived. It had to pay a little more money in royalties to the provincial governments and money in taxes to the federal government.
As a statistic, 75 per cent is frightening. But if you thought it was frightening from 1922 to 1957, just take a look at the costs today. When you add on the interest rates of today, suddenly there is disaster. What can we do in the long term loan pay-off situations with a high proportion going to interest rates? Let us take a very modest situation today. A home mortgage of $50,000 at an interest rate of 10 per cent-which you will never get-over a 30-year period, which was common ten years ago, would result in the home costing $202,000 if it were paid off over the 30-year period. So, $152,000 of that $202,000 was interest and only $50,000 was capital repayment.
My point is very clear. One can visualize it by buying one's home. Then apply it to a farmer. When a farmer goes out to expand his production, he finds that the latest rig in many of the farms in the east and west are these new modern harvest systems where the feed is handled in one monstrous system. These things cost about $250,000 to $400,000. The farmer no longer borrows $3,000 or $5,000, or sums like that. He knows that if he puts that $250,000 into that type of investment, it will increase his income by about $50,000 to $60,000 a year, that is, 20 per cent to 22 per cent. With that type of potential return, he can afford to borrow money at 6 per cent, 8 per cent or 10 per cent. I am going to use the figure of 8 per cent in this explanation to keep it constant. Eight per cent would mean that he would be paying $20,000 a year; but because he would have enough left over, he could pay off that $250,000 in eight
May 19, 1981

to ten years. Then he would have interest and capital payments together. He would then have the use of that equipment for 15 to 20 years, with a return of $50,000 or $60,000 a year, which would be very useful to him, and he could go ahead.
However, if the interest rates were to rise to 20 per cent, which they have, 20 per cent of $250,000 is $50,000 a year. The interest rates alone then match his increased income. He will never pay off his capital costs and he will have nothing left over for depreciation, repairs and maintenance. So obviously it is a "no go" situation. Any farmer who is foolish enough to take out a loan at 20 per cent on a productive type of enterprise like that with the hypothetical cash flow that I have described, is going into clear bankruptcy, I would say, in three or four years, before all his creditors close in on him.
Here there is a situation where the cause, as the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands said, is the key issue. Bankruptcy is a legal technique of trying to make adjustments in credit indebtedness. However, here we have a government policy in the interests of a theory that has been proved, quantitatively, over 10, 20 years, to be wrong. Interest techniques are still being used as an interest of monetary policy when we can show, quantitatively that it does not work. That does not mean that all monetary theory is flying away. It simply has a little bit of interest, and we do not know how much, but it has some. We are willing to listen to thoughtful proposals from the bank governor about how far we should go in using this. But we should not use the interest rate component as a technique of using the monetary policy.
When the committee of finance met with the bank governor, I asked him three questions on this subject. In each case he said that he did not have any evidence that the three reasons he gave for having this high interest rate policy were working. He knew that I was sitting there with the figures I obtained from his own shop showing just the opposite to be true. He could do nothing else but agree with me. He agreed to sit and listen to practical proposals from ordinary members of Parliament at how he could get around this.
Tonight is not the night, under this act or bill, to talk about monetary theory. I want to talk about those matters which deal with government policy, the fiscal side, that do have some chance of drastically reducing the number of bankruptcies.
These suggestions I am putting forward are not new. The philosophy is based on things that I have learned from watching events in the last 20 or 30 years and seeing those things work and from looking at other countries where they have worked. I have four proposals which are really proposals for lower interest rates on the fiscal side, and would not in any form take away ownership or attempt to subsidize. I would like to put forward a rational proposal under which one divides the costs at a fixed interest rate, the interest either going to the lender or the equity going to the company.
These four proposals are based on this principle. Massey-Ferguson let itself borrow to such a degree that the interest on its borrowings was greater than its income. This proud private company had to struggle mightily this last year or so, even to bending its knees and asking the government for help. It
Bankruptcy
begged the banks for help. It made a tremendous shift from a small equity portfolio of 18 million to 20 million shares up to about 220 million shares. It required a tremendous dilution of equity to get enough money to pay off part of that debt and to reduce its interest payment to a point where it could begin to have more income than the interest payments so it could pay off more of the capital or principal.
This thinking could be applied to all companies that use inventory based on loans. General Motors, Chrysler, and Ford are all going to go down the skids unless they adapt and do what Massey-Ferguson has done. The handwriting on the wall is clear for these large companies which followed the custom in the last 20 or 30 years of using the interest rate approach to give them leverage, to make money, using someone else's money at a lower cost than the income they will get. When interest rates rise beyond a certain point, that leverage is gone and instead it becomes the ruination of the whole financial structure.
I am going to make these four proposals one at a time in the hope that government members particularly will carry back to their committees-whether they be on agriculture, small business, trade, export-how this can be done, with the assurance that other people are succeeding in this technique and are actively going on to expand and carry out business. They can get away from this high interest rate threat which is imposed on us by theoretical approaches to the monetary system of keeping inflation down.
The first proposal, obviously coming from me, deals with farm credit. During the Diefenbaker administration, we tried to modernize farm credit by setting up the Farm Credit Corporation with great flexibility in the form of lending and repayment. To my sadness and regret, these techniques were not used too much because both the lenders, who were used to the old farm loan act, and the borrowers, who were used to the same type of lending on assets rather than on financial income, followed the old system. Because of that, they do not realize that in the legislation which allows us this flexibility one does not have to change the act to do what I am proposing. It is sufficient simply for the minister in charge of the Farm Credit Corporation, who is supposed to be the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), but I really do not know who is in charge, to use his initiative. He could go out and say that the type of interest rate we are now charging under the Farm Credit Corporation will destroy every farmer who uses it and destroy the act, and that is not the purpose of that act. He could say there is a proposal which will work, there is lots of evidence one can get that it does work, and that is it. One could simply tell a man on farm credit to come to the farm credit supervisor-and there are many scattered over the whole of Canada, well skilled in the costs of input going into farm production, well skilled in knowing the prices and returns-and put a hypothetical cash flow chart in front of him. With this type of investment we can demonstrate how much income he needs each year and how much he can afford to pay in interest and capital and still have something left.

May 19, 1981
Bankruptcy
An 8 per cent interest on a $250,000 loan will come to about $20,000 per year. The farmer will have enough left over to pay that interest and a big chunk of the capital each year. He can see the debt being paid off in eight or ten years. To get that kind of money without a subsidy requires a sweetener, and "sweetener" is the right word. We must hold this out to the lender, in this case the Farm Credit Corporation which has looked at the hypothetical cash flow and the corporation then agrees on a percentage that is paid off after the debt, a percentage of that new profit, not the old profit, on this new investment yielding a new return of $50,000 to $60,000 per year. The Farm Credit Corporation might put down the figure of 5 per cent; 5 per cent of $50,000 is $2,500 per year and 10 per cent would be $5,000 per year. If the farmer is getting, with all his debt and interest paid off, say, 10 per cent and is turning this over to the Farm Credit Corporation, even though he has paid them back the capital, he thinks, "I can easily afford $5,000 or $6,000 per year for the next ten or 15 years." He finds that for five or ten years, with the total amount of money received and the total amount invested-remember the money has been returned and the Farm Credit Corporation has already reinvested it-that could be a point where there is no subsidy, and at the same time you have not put that burden of front-end loading on the farmer, the burden of paying from the very beginning. You take the earnings half out of fixed cost or 8 per cent, and the balance after he has finished paying his debt for the period of the useful life expectancy of the equipment, that is 15 or 20 years at, say, 10 per cent. If you work out the mathematics and try them out at various rates, you will get a rate and a time period within which both sides are treated fairly. The Farm Credit Corporation will show no loss after a few years and the farmer will be way ahead of the game.
When you have a deal that is mutually beneficial to both parties, it is a good deal. When you have a deal where one side is always the winner, you can guess who the loser will always be in debt-credit relationships.
I put this forward in this House again in all seriousness, hoping it will get through to the farmers that an idea has been proposed that will remove the tremendous fear of the future that weighs on them like a ten-ton load. Instead of seeing all that they have fought for and built up over two or three generations being taken away because of high interest rates, they can see a way through where there is no subsidy from the public treasury over the long period but where there is an increase of wealth and productivity, which means more people are working and more taxes are coming in for the government.
The second proposal is roughly the same, and it is for small business development. Just like the Farm Credit Corporation, we have a business institution in the Bank of Canada which deals with small business loans. The idea of the Small Business Development Bond was put forward in the Crosbie budget. It was turned down in the MacEachen budget but was restored, as we all know. We are very grateful that members on the other side listened and restored it, even if it is only to the end
of this year. But we hope that it can be extended for another few years.
The same principle would apply as I suggested should be applied to the farmers. A small businessman can bring before the authorities a hypothetical cash flow which shows that if he borrows $500,000 and puts it to work, he can produce $60,000, $80,000, or $90,000 of revenue per year. If he is building on to something that he has already, this is quite possible. The same mathematics apply to determine what interest rate can be charged to make sure that he pays it back quickly.
I know of five or six instances in my riding where businessmen are choosing this route over the route followed by the small business development bond. The bond was not a bad idea, but this one is even better as we consider its implications. There is no loss of ownership. I am thinking of the areas of expansion in Manitoba and Saskatchewan around the potash mines and the uranium mines and the development of the cities of Saskatoon and Regina. In those cities the small businessmen who supply the mines employ the larger work force than do the mines. We need this type of thing to keep our development going; to get something going that we can sell and make money on; to employ more people and to provide more taxes. The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) should be very happy. No subsidy would be called for but new money would be coming in. It would reduce costs, bring in more revenue to the government and help balance the budget for these various proposals.
The third proposal is for export companies. This Parliament has been busy trying to figure out some way to build machinery to help the export industry. We have been thinking about legislating an international trading company run by the government. Quite frankly, I am very dubious that this is the best way to go. I think the better way would be to make it a sort of financial operation. Money for that long lead time that export companies need before they get a cash flow could be provided at a low interest rate and a big share could be taken as the sweetner. In other words, defer the take until the money comes back because there is no industry in the world at the present time that yields higher returns than the export business. A return of 25 per cent or 30 per cent is quite usual, but there is a delay factor involved. It is during this delay, which is necessary for building up the business and before the money comes in, that they have to be financed. Canadians are very good at this. We have the technical know-how; we take it with us; we teach and practise, but we make money out of it at the same time. I think that if export companies had access to a low interest rate or even a large proportion of shares for the government, then using the share approach of equity or by the sweetener approach plus a loan, by using the same hypothetical cash flow approach that I used in the case of small business and farmers, a great deal could be done to increase the wealth, not only of Canada but of all the nations we work with. Trade is beneficial to both sides. This should have the highest priority in terms of a worldwide sense of responsibility. I have watched what is being done in France, Germany, the United Kingdom, the United States and Japan using these principles.
May 19, 1981

I would think that we are smart enough to do this too. These enterprising businessmen who take an awful beating over the two or three-year loss period in order to get their business going, would be glad to share 25 per cent or 30 per cent of their business profits when they come, if they knew they were getting this money at a low rate of interest. The federal government has the machinery in the export legislation to do this.
The next proposal affects more people, and that is the matter of homes. I think the social revolution of the last 50 years has definitely included homes as a social need and a social necessity-not only health care, but homes. I believe all parties have accepted that homes are a part of the quality of life, of mental security, raising a family and all the rest of it. I think we should apply this same reasoning to a home. However, a home is slightly different. This proposal 1 want to put forward now is not new or original, it was made by leading businessmen. It lacks one thing, as hon. members will soon realize.
If you want to encourage young people to marry and live in a single dwelling so as to get away from the mental health problem associated with high rises and crowded ghettos, I would think money should be put out at about 6 per cent. You say to people that the government is part owner with you. In other words, the individuals own the home but the government has an interest because the government is lending the money at 6 per cent. However, if the individual sells the house in ten years, making a big capital gain in return for having that money at 6 per cent, the capital gain is shared 50-50 with the government.
Let me cite some statistics. Over the last 20 years, how long have people stayed in the same homes in the new industrial urban centres? It is not very long, there are even people making a living out of buying and selling homes, and living on their capital gains. There are ordinary individuals who buy homes, sell them and repeat the process. People have found out that this is one way to keep ahead of inflation. I am saying that in trying to help all the people a 6 per cent charge could be put on loans by the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. This corporation is a very efficient agency. We would say to them that by living in their homes for longer than ten years, they could make these homes their own. The stipulation could be that the money has to be paid back very quickly, as quickly as possible, in order to reduce the subsidy. But if this money was repaid within ten years, then half of the capital gain must accrue to the government. If that situation were put onto a hypothetical cash flow chart for the whole industry, you would find that the government-Canada Mortgage and Housing in this case-would make much more money from a 6 per cent charge plus the capital gains than it would ever make charging 15 per cent interest. A person making a big capital gain can afford to pay that a lot easier than he can afford to pay a 15 per cent or an 18 per cent mortgage. Paying these high interest rates is killing. It is front-end loading for 20 years of a person's life. The insecurity and the fear which comes
Bankruptcy
from that heavy mortgage and its high interest rate is not good for the mental health of Canadians.
To the persons who have not heard those four proposals before they may sound a little unique. But every one of them is based on old-fashioned principles of borrowing and lending. The principle of sharing in the profit from a common investment goes back long before the time of Christ. There is a human side to this which is very important to our modern industrial society.
In these proposals, export companies, small business and farm credit, big sectors of our economy, could be getting money at 8 per cent or whatever rate is decided, and money could be lent for housing at 6 per cent. There is no subsidy, and when you think of the things that are happening with expansion, you will see that the big winner in the whole thing is not the individual from whom you have taken away fear, having added tremendously to his income, it is the government because the individual is now paying more taxes with his big income. This would make the Minister of Finance and all the civil servants who think of nothing else but getting more money happy. I would think acceptance of this proposal would be found among the civil servants who must be concerned about what is happening to the country, and among the politicians who have some desire to come back here again.
If this interest rate question is not settled, it will not be just western Canada that will move, but the whole country. Not only will the farmers of Quebec and Ontario be rallying behind us, but the small businessmen from Newfoundland to British Columbia to the Yukon. The Liberal government is facing political disaster of the kind that will take the Liberal party, if it does not listen, out of existence for 50 years. It is not that I would not mind that happening, but in the interests of the country the government must start to think about the needs of the people.

speechtext:
You do not
sit in the House and applaud when hon. members make statements that people are better off today. The first thing taught in politics is that you never tell anyone he is better off. A politician has only one function, and that is to remind everyone that the poor guy is not making out so well. That is the first political rule. But to go out and say that the farmers are making so much money that they do not mind paying these interest rates or that people are so well off that, as we heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) say, their income is up 52 per cent, is political immaturity of the highest order. It is not the sign of a competent national politician who should be sitting in this House.
I say to the government, for heavens sake, if you can get either a proposal or a series of proposals on which there is no subsidy but, by an analysis of these hypothetical cash flows, you head off all these bankruptcies, create more productivity, more money for the tax collector, a balanced budget, more employment, and reduce social costs, then I would think that all these tweedledum and tweedledee arguments that we have

May 19, 1981
Adjournment Debate
been hearing in this House the past week should be forgotten. As a Canadian I certainly do not want to see or hear people who are professional politicians applauding when someone says that people are so well off they can afford these interest rates. First, it is naivete of the highest order and second, it is not true.
I would think that without saying any more, I have done what I could under the principles of this bill to head off the cause of these bankruptcies by putting these proposals forward. They can be acted on with existing legislation, and as long as you have the will to make sure ministers pass on these proposals to the civil servants, there would not be any opposition from them because they know what the people of Canada are thinking. We do not want to see a repeat of early history. After World War I, in 1919, people from the rural areas of Canada rose up with might and main and threw every Liberal and Conservative out of every seat they could and brought the progressive movement here. They settled the situation. They simply saw to it that the Bank Act had limited interest rate to 6 per cent. We have now got rid of that limit in the Bank Act on the promise that the banks would reduce interest rates. Now, by Jove, we had better get busy and save our own skins by coming up with some positive ideas and putting them into effect.
