subtopic: CANADA DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION-(A) PLANS FOR FUTURE ROLE. (B) CHA1RMANSH IP OF BOARD OF DIRECTORS
CANADA DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION-(A) PLANS FOR FUTURE ROLE. (B) CHA1RMANSH IP OF BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise this evening in connection with questions I have been raising on the floor of the House of Commons in concert with my colleagues, relating to the attempt on the part of the government to interfere in a political way with the operation of the Canada Development Corporation. We raised this question on a number of occasions. We were met with evasiveness and an attempt to circumvent the question on the part of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) who professed ignorance of the point we were making. At the same time that he was professing ignorance in this House, at which he is so adept in terms of parliamentary debate, he was being undercut by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in Calgary who at the same time
admitted quite candidly that a direct attempt was made to influence the selection of a new chairman of the board of directors. The Prime Minister admitted that the government did want their very good friend, Mr. Maurice Strong, to be the chairman of the board of directors of the Canada Development Corporation.
It subsequently developed and was learned that the government was not only satisfied with trying to promote Mr. Strong, a friend of the Liberal party and confidant of this government, the Prime Minister and his staff, for the top position in the Canada Development Corporation, but they were more ambitious than to simply want Mr. Strong as the chairman. They wanted to intrude into the board of directors a number of prominent Liberals, including Mr. William Mingo, from Atlantic Canada, who is active in Liberal party circles, and Mr. Paul Martin Jr., son of a former Liberal cabinet minister and leader of the government in the Senate, former high commissioner to the United Kingdom and a well known Liberal.
It is important to understand the consequences of exactly what is happening as a result of the government's heavy-handed, ham-handed attempt to harass each of the existing directors with regard to the government's wish to garner control of the board of directors of CDC. It is no secret that they have contacted each of the directors, putting pressure on them in a number of ways to convince them that they would be well advised to have certain people in certain positions on the board of directors, indeed to have certain members added to the board of directors.
This is quite contrary to the spirit and, in fact, the letter of the law passed by this Parliament creating the Canada Development Corporation. I went back into the record. 1 thought it would be appropriate at this time to review exactly what was said at the time the bill setting up the Canada Development Corporation was before the House of Commons. The then minister of finance who introduced and brought the bill before the House made a number of germane and pertinent statements with regard to the role of the CDC and the provisions of the bill. I quote from page 3639 of Hansard for February 22, 1971 where Mr. Benson stated:
But the CDC will also pursue profits, a word that apparently dismays the New Democrats, and the CDC will operate free of pressure by departments of the federal government . ..
The high quality of the board and the chief executive officer will ensure the corporation of the degree of independence in its operations which it will require to carry out its objectives effectively.
I underline the word "independence" which apparently now is not part of the government's thinking in terms of this corporation. I am glad to see the parliamentary secretary to the present minister here because his predecessor in that position, Pat Mahoney, whom he will recall, also spoke in that debate. On June 4, 1971, as reported at page 6391 of Hansard, speaking with respect to governmnent policy and government intentions regarding this legislation, he said:
May 19, 1981

Some critics of the CDC concept believe that any government participation in the corporation will be synonymous with interference in its operation. The best protection against such interference is a strong and independent board of directors chosen from the private sector. The bill explicitly contemplates their independence. I am confident that as soon as the CDC is incorporated a strong board will be readily formed and will assert its independence.
The word "independence" keeps coming up over and over again in the course of the debate. He went on to make reference to the fact that there had been some suggestion that the Canada Development Corporation could have some of the similar down sides and pitfalls experienced by the General Investment Corporation of Quebec. He pointed out that in the case of the General Investment Corporation of Quebec there was a situation in which investments were made by that corporation for what were regarded as national or social priorities in the province of Quebec. He said that the experience of that institution was one of the reasons why the Canada Development Corporation would be placed in the hands of a very independent board of directors and that when social or political objectives intervene in business decisions, business judgment suffers. I do not think anything could be clearer in terms of the government's position when the Canada Development Corporation was established. There was to be no room at all for any political interference with respect to the operation of that body, but now, without the benefit of a change in the legislation, without any attempt to change the act itself and by virtue of attempting to control the board of directors, the government is attempting to change the direction in which that corporation is going.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) has been critical of the corporation. The Prime Minister has been critical. I could quote statements made over the course of the last few months in which they have indicated that they want to change the Canada Development Corporation to make it the same kind of corporation as Petro-Canada. There has been a very substantial loss in the value of those shares. Canadian citizens, having invested money in good faith, are now finding that their investment is being prejudiced by the action of the government. I would like to hear the parliamentary secretary respond to this question.

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: CANADA DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION-(A) PLANS FOR FUTURE ROLE. (B) CHA1RMANSH IP OF BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, questions have been raised in the House concerning the role and responsibilities of the Canada Development Corporation and its relationship to the Government of Canada. The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) indicated rather clearly to the House in response to questions the principal factors which govern this relationship and which derive from the legislative mandate of the corporation.
Hon. members will recall that the CDC was established by a special act of Parliament in 1971 with a mandate expressed in the purpose and objectives of the corporation.
As stated in section 2 of the CDC Act:
The purpose of this act is to establish a corporation that will help develop and maintain strong Canadian-controlled and managed corporations in the private
Adjournment Debate
sector of the economy and will give Canadians greater opportunities to invest and participate in the economic development of Canada.
The corporate form established pursuant to the act provides for an investment company with responsibility for investment decision-making and managerial functions assigned to the corporation.
Hon. members will be aware that the successful investment activities of the CDC during the 1970s have led to a situation where the corporation is now a relatively large-scale holding company with a significant presence and developmental role in a variety of sectors of the Canadian economy. While the Government of Canada continues to be the largest single shareholder, the level of non-government ownership has substantially increased. The fact remains that the CDC continues to operate under the federal statute, and, as the Minister of Finance noted in the House, "The investment decisions of the corporation are still the responsibility of the corporation".
The corporate form adopted pursuant to the CDC Act provides for the affairs of the corporation to be entrusted to the board of directors and officers of the corporation who are accountable to the shareholders as a whole, both the public shareholder and the private shareholders. The act requires that the objects of the company shall be carried out in anticipation of profit and in the best interests of the shareholders as a whole. I should add that the act explicitly places responsibility for the election of a chairman of the board with the directors of the corporation.
In short, the nature of the relationship between the government and the CDC has been established by, and is subject to, legislation of the Parliament of Canada. The success of the initiative taken by the government in establishing the CDC is a matter of record. It has given Canadians greater opportunities to invest and participate in the economic development of Canada, and the government's confidence in the corporation has been shared by the large number of individual Canadians who have acquired shares in the CDC.

subtopic: METRIC CONVERSION-(A) MINISTER'S RESPONSIBILITIES TO SMALL BUSINESS. (B) REQUEST FOR REPEAL OF ENFORCEMENT ORDER
METRIC CONVERSION-(A) MINISTER'S RESPONSIBILITIES TO SMALL BUSINESS. (B) REQUEST FOR REPEAL OF ENFORCEMENT ORDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise as a result of an answer received in the House of Commons on April 13 of this year, as reported at pages 9198 and 9199 of Hansard. The question asked of the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) was this:
Would the minister responsible for small business advise this House whether he will or will not speak for small business, and address the concern of small business about forced metric conversion in Canada?
The minister responded in part:
As for me, I am convinced that I speak also for Canadian small businesses, and my contacts in the small business sector do not lead me to the same conclusions as the hon. member.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism is not aware of what is going on in the small business sector. As reported in the Peterborough Examiner of May 11, 1981:

May 19, 1981
Adjournment Debate
If the government goes ahead with the legislation, it will be against the will of the public.
That is the statement of the president of the Canadian Federation of Retail Grocers who surveyed 4,000 independent grocers in Canada and found that 85 per cent were opposed to forced metric conversion at this time in the retail food sector. The reason for this is the fact that the United States has now decided not to proceed with metric conversion in their retail food sector for at least ten years and perhaps never, and in Britain they have abolished the metric commission and have gone back to pints and quarts and miles per hour and Fahrenheit and pounds of meat when you purchase it at the store.
The minister is not speaking for either consumers or the independent grocers. Further, as reported in the Ottawa Citizen of Saturday, May 9, 1981:
Retailers on the Metric Commission's own working group on retail scales are upset about a government plan to introduce metric weights in food stores starting next January.
That is January 28, Mr. Speaker. The article goes on:
The group represents the views of retailers responsible for about 85 per cent of food sales in Canada ...
At a meeting of the group in Vancouver April 28, a "consensus" was reached that food retailers in the group strongly recommend a delay in metric conversion.
They recommended that the conversion should take place closer to the time the United States makes the switch. At present, the U.S. has no plans to go metric in the sale of food by weight.
To date the following organizations have condemned the costly and unjustified program to convert the food stores to metric in Canada: the Canadian Federation of Retailer Grocers, the Canadian Organization of Small Business; the Retail Council of Canada; Loblaws Companies Ltd; the Oshawa Group; Cooper Market Incorporated; the Independent Grocers' Association and Loeb Limited of Ottawa, to name but a few.
Thousands of letters of protest from concerned citizens, responding to the opportunity afforded them in The Canada Gazette where they had 60 days to make representations with regard to the order in council, have inundated the desks of the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouel-let), all stating very definitely that they do not wish to go metric at this time in the retail food sector.
The cost of conversion in the food stores will be astronomical and far in excess of any benefits that might result if in fact there are any benefits. According to the government's own 1974 study on the question, there are over 116,000 separate food scales that must be converted in Canada. The average conversion cost is $5,000, therefore the total cost for Canada will be in the region of $564 million to purchase metric weigh scales manufactured in foreign countries by multinational companies, and not one of those imported weigh scales is creating jobs here in Canada.
The metric advisory board in the United States made its recommendations ten years before the implementation of
metric in the retail food sector. The United States Congress listened and decided to defer metric in the retail food sector for at least ten years and maybe never. In 1980, Canadians imported $ 1.78-million worth of imperial weighed food from the United States, our major trading partner in fruit, vegetables, fish and meat. Not one pound or one ounce of that product was imported from the United States in metric.
Our next largest trading partner is Britain, with 16 per cent of our food products. Britain has abandoned its metric program as counterproductive, confusing and a waste of tax dollars. According to the 1970 Canadian government white paper on metric conversion prepared by the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), the whole spirit of conversion in Canada was to be voluntary. Why then is the retail food sector being victimized by the threat of fines of up to $5,000 and jail terms of up to two years for non-compliance, for simply publishing the price in imperial or carrying on trade in a measurement system which is perfectly familiar to our citizens?
In light of the foregoing which clearly indicates where the minister's duty should lie in responding accurately to the wishes of both the business sectors and the citizens of Canada, will the minister report to the House as soon as possible, because a six-month lead time is required for conversion by the food sector in order to implement metric in the retail food sector, on the results of his having looked into the possibility of this ill-advised program as he promised in the House of Commons? Will he finally admit that metric conversion is still ill-advised, counterproductive, hopelessly expensive, totally inconvenient and utterly against the wishes of the people of Canada?

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph Ferguson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister said in the House on April 13 that the Canadian small business sector benefits from metric conversion in Canada. This statement was based not only on statistical data but on direct accounts from small business people and organizations such as the Canadian Chamber of Commerce which represents all kinds of businesses, large and small.
First of all, I would like to point out that shopping habits will not change drastically when retail scales are converted to weighing in grams and kilograms. When consumers buy by sight, as they often do when they select a store wrapped roast, that fish or four pork chops, they will continue to shop exactly as they shopped before. The only change is when they actually order a specific quantity in grams or kilograms. A great deal of information is already available to help us adjust to ordering by kilogram. There are posters illustrating normal buying quantities in metric units, such as "a 500-gram steak for two".

A small company in Manitoba which contracts, processes and markets dry peas and other speciality crops is an example of a company which has gone metric. Albert Roy, owner of the company, said that conversion to metric has helped maintain good relations with important customers and to keep large accounts in foreign markets that deal only in metric. subtopic: ENERGY CONSERVATION-(A) ABUSE OF CANADIAN HOME INSULATION PROGRAM. (B) INVOLVEMENT OF LOCAL ORGANIZATIONS IN CERTIFICATION PROCESS
ENERGY CONSERVATION-(A) ABUSE OF CANADIAN HOME INSULATION PROGRAM. (B) INVOLVEMENT OF LOCAL ORGANIZATIONS IN CERTIFICATION PROCESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 1 I asked a question of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) regarding the Canadian Home Insulation Program. While recognizing that the program is essentially a step in the right direction in terms of energy
Adjournment Debate
conservation, and also recognizing that most of the contractors, firms and individuals involved are doing a first rate job, one must recognize that the program is being seriously abused by some unscrupulous entrepreneurs.
I have personally witnessed what can only be described as misleading advertising on a number of occasions, which gives the impression to the householder that the opportunity is free of charge, essentially with the exception of a nominal sum. What is often missing from the ads is a note that the grant received from the federal government will be considered taxable on next year's return. What must be said of the unscrupulous entrepreneurs is that they are defrauding citizens by asking them to sign blank application forms, giving the story that it is an application form which will be used in the next household. In a variety of fashions it is implied that these unscrupulous entrepreneurs are really an extension of the federal government, an arm of a particular government department.
Perhaps most serious of all is the incorrect information which is filed with the government department concerned. For example, entrepreneurs are possibly using six bags of insulation material in the home while charging the federal government for 30 bags. In some instances, where a very small house is being insulated, more insulation than is actually used is being charged for. The insulators may be charging for three hours of labour at the rate of $37.50 per hour, which is supposedly a very reasonable rate, while actually they are spending only 20 minutes on the job. As one would expect, some of the major offences are occurring in the major metropolitan areas of Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver. While the entrepreneur indicates to the home owner that he will be sending out a copy of the invoice eventually, seldom are these invoices ever received.
As I indicated, I have personally witnessed a number of examples of this fraudulent activity. The police and the government department have been notified, yet very little is being done. What is being done? The government department indicates that where a situation is reported by a home owner and fraudulent activity is suspected, an investigation takes place. In many cases the unsuspecting home owner is not certain whether 6 or 30 bags of insulation were used. In many cases he is not sure whether 20 minutes or 3 hours of work was done. What is being charged is never made known to the individual home owner because of misrepresented information and the invoice not being returned to the home owner. The minister indicated that certification would take place some time this fall. In the meantime, these fraudulent activities have occurred and, presumably, they will continue throughout the summer and into the autumn.
The minister also indicated that in terms of providing some inspection, the Royal Canadian Legion would be involved across the country. I am not suggesting that the Royal Canadian Legion is inefficient. I am certainly not saying anything against the legion. However, one would have to ask what is their expertise when it comes to inspecting home insulation and things of that nature.

May 19, 1981
Adjournment Debate
It seems to me that a much more reasonable approach would be to take advantage of the local inspection infrastructure which presently exists in Canadian communities across the country, and at least ask them to conduct spot checks to identify where certain firms are carrying out these fraudulent activities. Thank goodness they are few in number! Why are more firms not being prosecuted when, in fact, they are being brought to the attention of the department and the RCMP?
As this program is bound to continue in one form or another, I would like to suggest that the government consider involving various community groups and organizations where the opportunity would exist to provide local work for people in various communities. Labour would be provided locally as opposed to that on a national or, in some cases, multinational basis. The people involved would certainly feel more accountable. In other words, as the home owner would be approached by someone from his community, perhaps a community agency or group which would be identified, the possibility of fraudulent activities would certainly diminish. Again, it would do a great deal in terms of creating a sense and a need for conservation and for making our homes more energy efficient. It would do a great deal toward that by keeping the work itself within the communities across Canada.
In closing, I would suggest that the idea is certainly a good one, but it has been introduced in haste, without having been prepared with thought.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roy MacLaren (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ENERGY CONSERVATION-(A) ABUSE OF CANADIAN HOME INSULATION PROGRAM. (B) INVOLVEMENT OF LOCAL ORGANIZATIONS IN CERTIFICATION PROCESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in responding to the hon. member's earlier question, the minister stated that the overwhelming majority of insulation contractors are honest and are doing a good job. Where there have been abuses reported of the types outlined by the hon. member opposite, there have been investigations and, when required, prosecutions.
More specifically, since 1977, when the government first introduced the Canadian home insulation program, almost one million grants have been made. This has led to significant savings in Canadian home owners' heating costs, regardless of
the fuel used, and it has helped to move our country toward its objective of oil self-sufficiency.
Since the CHIP program was introduced, some 70,000 units have been selected for inspection across the country. As a result of those inspections, 36 contracting companies are presently under investigation. In addition, a further 17 companies are under police investigation, with charges having been laid against 11 companies. Here is clear evidence that the government has been monitoring the industry in order to protect consumers from possible abuse. By inspecting homes which have been insulated and by investigating abuses reported by consumers, the government is keeping this situation under review.
Further, in collaboration with the industry, the government has instituted a certification program which requires insulation contractors to pass examinations before being approved under the CHIP. As hon. members may be aware, the Royal Canadian Legion, as the hon. member has noted, is assisting the Canadian General Standards Board in providing the necessary facilities for the examination of insulation contractor personnel. The CGSB national certification program has already listed 900 of the total of over 2,000 contractors in its certification program. The mandatory date for the use of certified contractors will be November 1.
I should like to remind hon. members that the National Energy Program has a goal to upgrade insulation in 70 per cent of Canadian homes by 1987. The certification program contributes in a real way to the effective administration of the CHIP.
These facts are indicative of the careful supervision being given to the home insulation program and of the government's determination to ensure that Canadians are guaranteed good products and good work. It is a large program and it is one which will pay large dividends in terms of energy conservation and fuel savings for home owners.
